Khorol River: The fortified capital city on the banks of the Khorol River, Velikoye has served as the seat of Moscavian governance since before the Blinding. The Tsar's palace sits atop the highest bluff overlooking the Khorol River, its white stone towers visible for miles across the frozen plains, and its halls are warmed by great iron stoves fed with birchwood from the surrounding forests.

- The Tsar's throne room in Velikoye's palace is built with vaulted ceilings high enough to accommodate Owl-folk in flight, and its great windows face north toward the frozen boreal forest, a reminder of the wilderness that shaped this land.
- The Night Court convenes in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's Palace in Velikoye, which has been specially modified with roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges at every window to accommodate the Owl-folk advisors who serve upon it.
- The central square of Velikoye, known as the Nightmarket, hosts a thriving nocturnal bazaar where merchants of every description set up stalls by lantern light, their wares ranging from salted fish and dried herbs to carved bone trinkets and enchanted talismans.

- Recruits undergo rigorous training at the Frostmere Training Grounds north of Velikoye, where they learn formation flying, aerial reconnaissance, and the use of light crossbows and javelins adapted for Owl-folk physiology.
- Non-Owl-folk who served in the pre-Blinding Moscavian military were not admitted into the Frostwing Host, as the Night Court determined that the force's effectiveness depended on uniform Owl-folk capabilities.
- Every soldier in the Frostwing Host is an Owl-folk, reflecting the Night Court's policy of integrating the transformed population into every pillar of Moscavian society.
- The Host's command structure mirrors Moscavian civic hierarchy, with senior Snowy Owl-folk officers holding the highest ranks and eared owl-form soldiers typically serving in auxiliary or logistical roles.
- The Frostwing Host has become a source of pride for the Tsardom, demonstrating to neighboring kingdoms that the transformed population is not weakened but rather possesses unique strategic advantages.
- The Host answers directly to the Night Court for deployment decisions along the Tsardom's borders, including the northern glacier approaches, the eastern marshland corridors, and the western mountain passes into Valdren.
Velikoye Culture (lore, usually called the Velikoye way):
- The Blinding transforms the ruling dynasty and reshapes Velikoye's population as Owl-folk rise to dominance.
- A courtesan's wattle at the winter festival gala ignites the city's most enduring fashion trend among the Owl-folk nobility.
- The Nightmarket's Wattle Row opens, formalizing the wattle trade and signaling its full acceptance into Velikoye's daily life.
- The living culture of Velikoye, the frozen capital of Moscavia, shaped by centuries of human tradition and transformed by the Blinding into a society shared between humans and Owl-folk, where night is the true hour of life and the wattle adornment stands as its most visible symbol of status and beauty.

- The Night Court: The governing body of Moscavia, convened in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's Palace, staffed by Owl-folk advisors.
- The Tsar, once human, is now always an Owl-folk by the succession laws established after the Blinding.
- The Blinding is regarded by some scholars as divine retribution, though no single church claims authority over its meaning.

## Format
Reply with only one JSON object, shaped exactly like this example:
{"name": "...", "aka": [{"name": "...", "tag": "common", "everyday": true}], "tag": "...", "facts": [{"category": "description", "text": "One claim, in a full sentence.", "since": "YEAR", "held_by": null}, {"category": "general", "text": "Another claim.", "held_by": null}], "names": [{"name": "...", "kind": "place", "tag": "...", "in": null, "aka": []}], "in": [{"entry": "<an entry's name>", "role": "a few words"}], "file_into": [{"entry": "<an entry's name>", "role": null}], "elsewhere": [{"entry": "<an entry's name>", "text": "A claim mainly about that entry, in a full sentence.", "held_by": null}]}

- "name": the place's name. Use the name already decided.
- "facts": between 8 and 12 facts, one claim each. "category" is one of: description, history, law, general.
- "since" is optional. Give it only when a fact started at a known time, and only as a year of this calendar, as a bare number no later than 1000; "YEAR" in the example stands for that number. Leave it out otherwise: never a phrase like "childhood" or "ten years ago".
- Leave "since" out for an inherent trait that has always been true -- a species, the appearance someone is born with, a lifelong temperament -- rather than dating it to the present year.
- "aka": other names for this place itself, if it has any, each {"name", "tag", "everyday"}. "tag" is "proper" for another formal name, or "common" for what people in the world actually call it day to day (a short form, a nickname). Set "everyday" true on the one common name people use most, false on the rest. "name" stays the most formal name. An empty list is fine.
- "names": after the facts, every proper name your facts use, other than this place's own: people, places, peoples and species, named events, named groups and named objects, new or already in the world. Each is {"name", "kind", "tag", "in", "aka"}: "name" in full, as your facts write it; "kind" one of character, place, species, race, event, item, lore (a country, realm or city is a place; a faith, order, council, guild, culture, field of knowledge or magic, law, script or language is lore); "tag" what it is, as for the place; "in" the name of the entry it belongs in (this place, an entry listed above, or another of your names), or null; "aka" any other names your facts use for the same thing. Proper names only: never a description such as "the postmaster", "a war" or "his mother", nor a title on its own such as "the Tsar" or "the High Bishop", nor a people's adjective such as "Moscavian" on its own -- but "Yelena" in "his mother Yelena" is a name. An empty list is fine.
- Only named things become entries. A role, rank or office (a harbour master, the keeper of the seals), a topic (grain tariffs, winter trade) or a practice without a proper name of its own (the evening bell, night sessions) is never one of the "names": it stays a fact of the place.
- Keep "facts" to claims mainly about the place itself: a claim mainly about another entry goes in "elsewhere".
- "elsewhere": after the names, what you would add about other entries, each {"entry", "text", "held_by"}: "entry" the entry's name as the list of entries near this one writes it, or a new name you also list in "names"; "text" one claim in a full sentence. Never the place itself. An empty list is fine.
- A claim that ties another entry to the place ("it is taught at X", "unlike X, it...", "X uses it") is the place's own: it goes in "facts". "elsewhere" is only for what another entry's page should say even if the place didn't exist.
- "tag": one or two words for what the place is, such as river, ruler, custom, institution, regiment, capital or doctrine. Use a tag from the tags in use when one fits; make a new one only when none does.
- "in": the entries listed above that the place belongs in, each {"entry", "role"}: "entry" the entry's name as the list writes it; "role" a few words for how it belongs there ("flows through", "sovereign", "practitioner", "branch of", "taught here"), or null. A thing can be in several entries: a road in each realm it crosses, a temple in its city and in the faith it serves. Only entries from the list; an empty list is fine.
- "file_into": the entries listed above that belong in this place: its parts, members, branches or what it holds, each {"entry", "role"}, "role" how that entry belongs in this place, or null. Never an entry you put in "in". Only entries from the list; an empty list is fine.

No commentary, no markdown fences, just the JSON object.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon: The Order of the Talon-Scribe maintains its central administration at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velikoye, from which it oversees rune-working across the entire Tsardom.

Mentioned elsewhere in the world (keep these true):

- The Order of the Talon-Scribe (lore, about; usually called Talon-Scribe Order): An institution of state-appointed Owl-folk rune-practitioners who maintain public inscriptions across the Tsardom and advise the Night Court on magical matters, headquartered in the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velikoye.
- The Order of the Talon-Scribe (lore, timeline; usually called Talon-Scribe Order): The Order's motto, carved above the entrance to the Academy of the Chiseled Moon, reads 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures,' a phrase attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV's decree.
- The Order of the Talon-Scribe (lore, timeline; usually called Talon-Scribe Order): The Order's central administration is housed in the stone hall known as the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in the inner quarter of Velikoye, where the institution's archives hold copies of every rune pattern approved for public use.
- Anastasiya Koroleva (character, relationship; usually called Chief Scribe Koroleva): She is the foster-mother of three Novice scribes taken into the Academy after the Blinding orphaned them — children of human parents who were transformed alongside their Owl-folk spouses, leaving the young ones with no human family remaining in Velikoye.
- Anastasiya Koroleva (character, background; usually called Chief Scribe Koroleva): She was already a practicing rune-scribe of some renown when the Blinding struck, having completed her apprenticeship at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon under Chief Scribe Yelena Volkova in 982, and she survived the transformation seated at her carving desk in the eastern wing, her half-finished mold still wet in its frame.
- The Frostmere Runic Array (place, general; usually called The Frostmere Array): A permanent garrison of twelve Talon-Scribe practitioners lives at the Array's central waypoint, the Stonehollow Shelter, rotating every six months with fresh carvers from the Academy.
- The Frostmere Runic Array (place, history; usually called The Frostmere Array): The initial array was established in 972 under the direction of the Velikoye Rune Academy, following a devastating glacial surge that destroyed several northern villages and prompted the Tsardom to invest in long-term seismic monitoring.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe (lore, usually called Talon-Scribe Order):
- The Blinding renders human practitioners unable to practice rune-working, and the craft passes into the hands of transformed Owl-folk scribes.
- Tsar Dmitry IV founds the Night Court in response to the Blinding, establishing nocturnal governance for the transformed realm.
- The Order's highest-ranking member is the Chief Scribe, a title appointed by the Tsar from among the most experienced and politically trusted Owl-folk practitioners in the realm.
- Tsar Dmitry IV issues the Scribing Decree, formally establishing the Order of the Talon-Scribe to preserve rune-lore and mandate public inscription maintenance.
- Novice scribes under Order training are required to spend three years in apprenticeship before they may carve any rune intended for public display, during which they practice on designated training stones within the Academy's courtyard.
- The Scribing Decree of 998 mandates that every town square, river crossing, and border marker within the Tsardom must bear at least one active rune inscription maintained by an Order-registered scribe.
- The Order serves as the primary advisory body to the Night Court on all matters pertaining to runic magic, including the approval of new rune designs, the assessment of magical hazards, and the investigation of dormant or corrupted rune sites left over from the era of human practitioners.
- The Order maintains a roster of registered scribes across every provincial center of the Tsardom, each one licensed to carve public-facing runes after completing a rigorous three-year apprenticeship.
Anastasiya Koroleva (character, usually called Chief Scribe Koroleva):
- She is a short, stocky eared Owl-folk at three feet even, with broad shoulders and a wingspan of eight feet, her plumage a muted tawny-brown that fades to silvery-grey along her breast and the leading edges of her flight feathers.
- Her facial disc is a pale, creamy gold, wider than most Snowy Owl-folk faces, and her eyes are a deep, burnt-orange — unusual enough among the predominantly pale-eyed Owl-folk of Velikoye that courtiers sometimes mistake her for a foreigner until they hear her accent.
- Her ear tufts are long and asymmetrical — the left one drooping slightly past her jaw while the right stands erect, giving her profile an uneven, almost lopsided character that has become recognizable across the Order.
- She is meticulous and conservative in her rune-work, refusing to approve any design that deviates from established patterns without extensive field-testing, and she has clashed repeatedly with younger scribes who advocate for experimental modifications to old protective runes.
- Born in Velikoye as a human in 958, Anastasiya was the daughter of a minor boyar family with deep but impoverished Moscavian roots — pure-line on both sides, her grandfather a distant cousin of the Rurikovich dynasty itself.
- Appointed Chief Scribe by Tsar Dmitry IV in the spring of 997, she was the first to hold the title since the Blinding — a deliberate choice by Dmitry to signal that the Order would continue its work uninterrupted, staffed by transformed practitioners rather than the human scribes who had preceded them.
- Her talons are unusually strong and precise for an Owl-folk of her size, a trait she attributes to years of daily chiseling work before the Blinding, when her human hands had already been calloused from the craft — her transformed talons retaining that muscle memory in their density and dexterity.
- As Chief Scribe, she holds the authority to declare any rune site in the Tsardom corrupted or dormant, dispatching investigation teams and ordering repairs or resealing — a power she has wielded sparingly but decisively, closing three major pre-Blinding sites in the first two years of her tenure.

- "name": the lore's name. Use the name already decided.
- "facts": between 8 and 12 facts, one claim each. "category" is one of: general.
- "since" is optional. Give it only when a fact started at a known time, and only as a year of this calendar, as a bare number no later than 1000; "YEAR" in the example stands for that number. Leave it out otherwise: never a phrase like "childhood" or "ten years ago".
- Leave "since" out for an inherent trait that has always been true -- a species, the appearance someone is born with, a lifelong temperament -- rather than dating it to the present year.
- "aka": other names for this lore itself, if it has any, each {"name", "tag", "everyday"}. "tag" is "proper" for another formal name, or "common" for what people in the world actually call it day to day (a short form, a nickname). Set "everyday" true on the one common name people use most, false on the rest. "name" stays the most formal name. An empty list is fine.
- "names": after the facts, every proper name your facts use, other than this lore's own: people, places, peoples and species, named events, named groups and named objects, new or already in the world. Each is {"name", "kind", "tag", "in", "aka"}: "name" in full, as your facts write it; "kind" one of character, place, species, race, event, item, lore (a country, realm or city is a place; a faith, order, council, guild, culture, field of knowledge or magic, law, script or language is lore); "tag" what it is, as for the lore; "in" the name of the entry it belongs in (this lore, an entry listed above, or another of your names), or null; "aka" any other names your facts use for the same thing. Proper names only: never a description such as "the postmaster", "a war" or "his mother", nor a title on its own such as "the Tsar" or "the High Bishop", nor a people's adjective such as "Moscavian" on its own -- but "Yelena" in "his mother Yelena" is a name. An empty list is fine.
- Only named things become entries. A role, rank or office (a harbour master, the keeper of the seals), a topic (grain tariffs, winter trade) or a practice without a proper name of its own (the evening bell, night sessions) is never one of the "names": it stays a fact of the lore.
- Keep "facts" to claims mainly about the lore itself: a claim mainly about another entry goes in "elsewhere".
- "elsewhere": after the names, what you would add about other entries, each {"entry", "text", "held_by"}: "entry" the entry's name as the list of entries near this one writes it, or a new name you also list in "names"; "text" one claim in a full sentence. Never the lore itself. An empty list is fine.
- A claim that ties another entry to the lore ("it is taught at X", "unlike X, it...", "X uses it") is the lore's own: it goes in "facts". "elsewhere" is only for what another entry's page should say even if the lore didn't exist.
- "tag": one or two words for what the lore is, such as river, ruler, custom, institution, regiment, capital or doctrine. Use a tag from the tags in use when one fits; make a new one only when none does.
- "in": the entries listed above that the lore belongs in, each {"entry", "role"}: "entry" the entry's name as the list writes it; "role" a few words for how it belongs there ("flows through", "sovereign", "practitioner", "branch of", "taught here"), or null. A thing can be in several entries: a road in each realm it crosses, a temple in its city and in the faith it serves. Only entries from the list; an empty list is fine.
- "file_into": the entries listed above that belong in this lore: its parts, members, branches or what it holds, each {"entry", "role"}, "role" how that entry belongs in this lore, or null. Never an entry you put in "in". Only entries from the list; an empty list is fine.

No commentary, no markdown fences, just the JSON object.

VASHA
His talons grip the edge of the basalt archway as he surveys the entrance hall below, the massive stone chamber opening out before him like the inside of some great frozen cave. Pairs of talon-gripping ledges line every wall at regular intervals—human engineering retrofitted, he notes with a practiced eye, the metal brackets bolted into stone that was never meant to hold anything of the sort. The pillars carved to resemble owl talons gripping bundles of grain rise like the ribs of some ancient beast, and the vaulted ceiling disappears into shadow above.

He drops from the ledge in a controlled glide, his flight feathers adjusting mid-air to slow his descent until his talons touch the flagstones with barely a sound.

The moment Vasha's talons meet the flagstones, the scale of the place hits him again—it always does, every time he comes here, the way a cathedral hits you when you step inside from the street. A cluster of apprentice scribes passes in the opposite direction—smaller birds, barely clearing two and a half feet, their downy chest feathers still ruffled with the nervous energy of early training. One of them, an eared owl with mismatched tufts, nearly walks into a pillar trying to stare at Vasha's wingspan. A supervising scribe—a stout snow owl with a chipped talon and the weary patience of someone who has done this a thousand times—gently redirects the apprentice with a nudge of her wing and a low, chittering admonishment.

The corridor beyond the great hall splits into three branches, each marked with carved wooden signs that hang from iron chains bolted into the stone. Left leads toward the training grounds, its distant sound of talon-on-stone tapping carrying faintly through the passage. Right leads deeper into the building, toward the archives, and the faint smell of old parchment and iron bindings seeps from that direction like something alive. Straight ahead, the central corridor stretches on, wider than the others, lit by larger lamps and lined with closed doors. This is the administrative wing—the heart of the Order's daily machinery.

Halfway down the corridor, a door stands slightly ajar, warm lamplight spilling across the flagstones in a golden stripe. A metal plaque beside it reads CHIEF SCRIBE in blocky, utilitarian letters, and beneath that, in smaller script: Office of Anastasiya Koroleva, by appointment of Tsar Dmitry IV. The sound of talons on a writing surface—quick, precise, unhesitating—drifts through the gap.

facts.text: The Khorol River is a wide, slow-moving waterway that bisects the city of Velikoye from south to north before emptying into the frozen northern marshlands.

Its waters are shallow and ice-choked for eight months of the year, from late November to the first thaw of April, turning the riverbed into a solid sheet of ice capable of bearing heavy carts and mounted riders.
The Khorol has served as a natural defensive barrier for Velikoye since the city's founding as the seat of the first Tsar of Moscavia.

During the frozen months, the Khorol's surface becomes a vital ice road connecting Velikoye to the outlying provinces and the northern trade routes, replacing the riverboat traffic that dominates the warmer months.

Many residents of Velikoye believe the Khorol freezes more thoroughly each winter since the Blinding of 994, though this claim is debated by scholars who argue the river has always frozen to similar depths and that modern measurements simply use more rigorous methods.

The Frostwing Host patrols the Khorol's frozen surface as part of its nightly perimeter patrol, with watchtower crews assigned to specific sectors of the ice road to prevent smuggling and monitor border traffic.
The river's southern bank in Velikoye is lined with timber-framed warehouses and dockyards, many converted from their original purpose as riverboat terminals to serve the ice-road trade in winter.
At the mouth of the Khorol, where it meets the northern marshlands, stands the Khorol Mouth Stones, a circle of twelve ancient granite slabs believed to ward the capital against marsh spirits.
The river's banks in Velikoye are reinforced with rune-carved stone embankments, maintained by the Order of the Talon-Scribe, which are said to strengthen the ice and prevent spring flooding.
During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Frostwing Host conducts its ceremonial mass flight above the bonfires lit on the Khorol's ice, a spectacle visible from every point in the capital.
Birchwood from the forests along the Khorol's banks supplies the great iron stoves of the Tsar's Palace and many of Velikoye's public buildings throughout the long winter months.

elsewhere.text: The Khorol River bisects Velikoye from south to north, its frozen surface serving as the city's primary winter trade artery and its banks lined with timber warehouses and dockyards.

The Host's patrol routes along the frozen Khorol River are meticulously planned to ensure continuous coverage of the ice road and the riverbank warehouses, which store goods bound for the outlying provinces.
The rune-site at the Khorol River's mouth, where it meets the northern marshlands, is the oldest known rune-stone circle in the Tsardom.
Rune-carved stone embankments along the Khorol's banks in Velikoye are among the most publicly visible applications of runic magic in daily life, maintained by the Order of the Talon-Scribe.
The Khorol River serves as both a transportation artery and a natural defensive barrier for the Tsardom, most critically protecting the capital Velikoye from southern incursions.

facts.text: The Khorol River is a wide, slow-moving waterway that bisects the fortified capital city of Velikoye, flowing from the northern boreal forests southward past the Tsar's palace before emptying into the frozen marshlands beyond the city's walls.
The river's banks are reinforced with granite embankments and lined with timber-paved walkways that serve as the city's primary east-west thoroughfares during the warmer months.
Its waters run clear and cold year-round, fed by snowmelt from the northern glaciers and filtered through the deep granite aquifers beneath the steppe.

From late November to April, the Khorol freezes solid across its entire width, creating a continuous ice road that connects Velikoye's inner city to the outer districts, the northern trade routes, and the provinces beyond.

Many residents of Velikoye believe the Khorol freezes more thoroughly each winter since the Blinding, though scholars debate whether this is a genuine trend or a perceptual bias shaped by collective memory of the event.

The Khorol served as a natural defensive barrier for the human settlement of Velikoye for centuries before the Blinding, its deep waters and muddy banks making a direct assault on the city's bluff fortifications impractical.

After the Blinding, the frozen surface of the Khorol became a patrol corridor for the Frostwing Host, which deploys soldiers along the ice to monitor the riverbanks and the city's northern approaches.

During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Khorol's ice serves as the stage for the festival's most spectacular element: hundreds of Frostwing soldiers take to the air above the bonfires lit along the river's frozen surface, tracing synchronized flight patterns visible across the city.

The river's mouth, where it empties into the marshlands south of Velikoye, is marked by the Khorol Mouth Stones — a circle of twelve ancient granite slabs believed to ward against marsh spirits and protect the capital's southern flank.

By decree of the Night Court, all bridges spanning the Khorol within Velikoye's city limits must be fitted with talon-gripping ledges and wide enough to accommodate Owl-folk in flight, a requirement that necessitated the reconstruction of several older human-era bridges in the years following the Blinding.

The river's ice road is maintained through the winter by teams of laborers who clear snow and resurface thin patches with a slurry of water and finely crushed stone, ensuring safe passage for merchants, couriers, and military convoys traveling to and from the capital.

In summer, the unfrozen Khorol becomes the city's primary commercial artery, with barges and flatboats carrying grain, timber, salt, and manufactured goods between Velikoye's river docks and the trading posts upstream.

elsewhere.text: The Khorol River freezes solid from late November until April, turning the city's waterfront into a vast ice road that connects Velikoye to the outlying provinces and the northern trade routes.
The Host's watchtowers along the Khorol River and the walls of Velikoye serve as both defensive positions and roosting stations, where soldiers rest during daylight hours before deploying at dusk.
The Host patrols the frozen surface of the Khorol River as part of its routine nocturnal surveillance of Velikoye's perimeter, ensuring no unauthorized passage crosses the ice.

During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Frostwing Host conducts a ceremonial mass flight over Velikoye that is considered the visual centerpiece of the festival, with hundreds of soldiers tracing synchronized patterns above the bonfires on the Khorol's ice.

The Khorol River, which had served as a defensive asset for centuries under human rule, continued to serve as a natural moat for Velikoye after the Blinding, its frozen surface now patrolled by Owl-folk sentries of the Frostwing Host.

The Khorol Mouth Stones, the oldest known rune-site in the Tsardom, stand at the river's mouth as a testament to the pre-Blinding runic traditions that continue to flourish under Owl-folk stewardship.

parse.name: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon

facts.text: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a grand stone hall located in the inner quarter of Velikoye, serving as the central administration and headquarters of the Order of the Talon-Scribe.

The building is carved from pale granite quarried from the Khorol River basin, its walls etched with thousands of approved rune patterns that serve both as decorative display and as working magical wards protecting the complex from weather and interference.
Above the main entrance, a deep-cut rune archway bears the Order's motto — 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures' — attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV's decree.

The Academy was established in 997 by Tsar Dmitry IV following the issuance of the Scribing Decree, which formalized the Order of the Talon-Scribe and mandated the preservation and maintenance of rune-working across the Tsardom.

The eastern wing of the Academy houses a vast archive containing copies of every rune pattern approved for public use, organized in carved stone catalogues that can be read by any registered scribe through a simple touch of the talon.

Novice scribes admitted to the Academy are required to spend three years in apprenticeship, during which they practice their craft on designated training stones set into the courtyard's flagstone floor, each apprentice assigned a personal stone that bears their name.

The western wing contains workshops where senior scribes carve rune-stones for provincial assignments, their workspaces arranged in a long hall lit by bioluminescent moss cultivated in shallow stone troughs along the windowsills.

The upper floors of the Academy are reserved for roosting quarters and scriptoriums, with wide windows facing north toward the frozen forests, designed to accommodate the nocturnal habits of the Owl-folk who staff the institution.

Under the authority vested by the Scribing Decree, the Chief Scribe who presides at the Academy holds the power to declare any rune site in the Tsardom corrupted or dormant, dispatching investigation teams and ordering repairs or resealing as necessary.

The Academy also functions as the coordination center for the Corrupted Rune Site Investigation branch, from which field teams are dispatched to assess and neutralize dangerous pre-Blinding inscriptions that have fallen into disrepair.

A residential wing on the Academy's south side provides quarters for the Chief Scribe, senior administrators, and the three Novice scribes who live under the direct care of Chief Scribe Koroleva following the Blinding.

The courtyard at the heart of the Academy is enclosed by a colonnade of rune-carved pillars, each one a different protective pattern, creating a space where magical interference is minimized and apprentices can carve without outside disruption.

elsewhere.text: The Order's central administration is housed in the stone hall known as the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in the inner quarter of Velikoye, where the institution's archives hold copies of every rune pattern approved for public use.

As Chief Scribe, Anastasiya Koroleva holds court and conducts administrative business from the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velikoye, overseeing the training of Novice scribes and the maintenance of the institution's archives.
The investigation arm operates under the authority of the Academy of the Chiseled Moon, drawing assignments from the Chief Scribe and coordinating with registered scribes in the field.

parse.name: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon

facts.text: A massive stone building in the inner quarter of Velikoye, the Academy of the Chiseled Moon serves as the central administrative headquarters of the Order of the Talon-Scribe.
The Academy's walls are built of pale grey granite quarried from the banks of the Khorol River, its surface worn smooth by decades of northern wind and centuries of accumulated frost.
The building's facade rises three stories high, its windows fitted with wide wooden ledges and iron talon-gripping bars in accordance with the Night Court's retrofitting decrees.

Above the main entrance, carved in deep relief into a lintel of black basalt, the Order's motto reads: 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures' — a phrase attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV's Scribing Decree.

The Academy was established in the spring of 997 by Tsar Dmitry IV as the central seat of the newly reformed Order of the Talon-Scribe, replacing the older human-era Scribing Guild that had operated from a smaller hall on the same site before the Blinding.
Under the Scribing Decree of 998, the Academy holds the authority to approve, reject, or modify any rune design proposed for public use anywhere in the Tsardom.

The Academy's eastern wing contains a long gallery of practice desks where Novice scribes spend their first years learning the Deep-Cutting technique on designated training stones before they are permitted to carve any public-facing rune.

The western wing houses the Order's archives, a vast collection of stone-bound ledgers and carved tablets documenting every rune pattern approved for public use since the founding of the Scribing Guild in the pre-Blinding era.
The courtyard at the Academy's center is paved with large granite slabs, many of which bear half-finished or practice runes carved by generations of apprentice scribes.

The Academy maintains a roster of all registered scribes across the Tsardom's provincial centers, tracking each practitioner's apprenticeship completion, certification examinations, and assigned maintenance sites.

A resident staff of twelve senior scribes conducts daily training, examination, and administrative work at the Academy, reporting to the Chief Scribe in all matters of rune approval and site investigation.
The Academy's basement vaults store sealed samples of corrupted or dormant rune-stones recovered from pre-Blinding sites across the Tsardom, preserved in iron-lined cases for study and reference.

elsewhere.text: The Order of the Talon-Scribe maintains its central administration at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velikoye, from which it oversees rune-working across the entire Tsardom.
Chief Scribe Koroleva conducts her duties and holds office at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in the inner quarter of Velikoye.
The investigation arm of the Order operates under the authority of the Academy of the Chiseled Moon, from which assignments are drawn and field teams are dispatched.

facts.text: Plumage Signaling is a system of nonverbal communication used during formal deliberations of the Night Court, allowing senior advisors to express opinions and reactions through precise movements of their feathers without interrupting spoken debate.

The practice was developed in the earliest days of the Night Court following the Blinding of 994, when Owl-folk rulers and their advisors needed efficient ways to communicate complex political positions during long nocturnal sessions.

Senior advisors trained in Plumage Signaling can signal agreement by a slow downward sweep of their shoulder feathers, objection by a sharp upward ruffling of the neck plumulary, and urgency by a rapid fanning of the tail feathers.
More nuanced signals exist for qualified agreement, conditional objection, and varying degrees of urgency, mastered only after years of training under the Talon-Scribe Order's communication scholars.

During extended winter sessions that last the full length of the night, advisors may use Plumage Signaling to suggest brief recesses or to indicate that a particular advisor's talons are cramping from gripping the roosting perches, prompting a rotation.

Only senior advisors serving on the Night Court are expected to demonstrate proficiency in Plumage Signaling; junior officials and scribes observe the practice but do not participate in it during formal deliberations.

The Tsar may use Plumage Signaling to quietly direct the flow of debate without publicly stating his preference, allowing the appearance of impartial presiding while subtly steering discussion toward matters he considers most pressing.

Chief Scribe Koroleva maintains an unofficial personal log of notable Plumage Signaling exchanges during Night Court sessions, cross-referencing them with the official decrees she transcribes to preserve a private record of the deliberation's unspoken undercurrents.

Snowy Owl-folk who have not served on the Night Court sometimes practice Plumage Signaling as a mark of cultural refinement, though untrained practitioners frequently send mixed or unintentional signals that can cause confusion in social gatherings.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon includes a mandatory course on Plumage Signaling for all Owl-folk students, taught alongside rune-practitioner fundamentals, because the Night Court frequently discusses matters of state that involve runic investigations and rune site management.

A rare and prestigious signal known as the Frostwing Fan — a simultaneous fanning of all flight and tail feathers — may be used by a senior advisor to call for an immediate and binding vote, bypassing further debate, though its use is so rare that most advisors in the year 1000 have never witnessed it.

Human citizens of Moscavia, even those with Owl-folk relatives, are not trained in Plumage Signaling and can only observe its use during the rare public audiences held in the Grand Hall's gallery, where a court interpreter stands ready to translate the feather-language aloud.

elsewhere.text: The Night Court's formal sessions employ Plumage Signaling as an auxiliary communication system, allowing senior advisors to express agreement, objection, and urgency through controlled feather movements during deliberations.

Chief Scribe Koroleva maintains an unofficial private log recording notable exchanges of Plumage Signaling observed during Night Court deliberations, preserving a hidden record of the unspoken dynamics beneath official proceedings.

facts.text: Plumage Signaling is a sophisticated system of nonverbal communication used by senior advisors of the Night Court during formal deliberations.
It allows advisors to express agreement, objection, and urgency through subtle movements of their feathers without interrupting the spoken debate.
Each advisor possesses a unique repertoire of feather gestures that they have trained for years to perform with the precision required for nuanced political discourse.

The system was developed in the early months following the establishment of the Night Court, as a practical necessity to avoid the chaos of multiple advisors speaking over one another in a chamber designed for silence.
Agreement is signaled by a slow, controlled fanning of the tail feathers — spread wide and held steady for a full breath before settling back into a neutral position.

Objection is conveyed by a sharp, upward flick of the crest feathers atop the head, accompanied by a brief ruffling of the shoulder plumes, creating a visual flash that is easily readable even across a dimly lit hall.
Urgency is expressed by a rapid vibrating of the primary flight feathers, held partially extended at the sides, producing a faint audible tremor in addition to the visual signal.
Senior advisors train in Plumage Signaling at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon beginning in their late adolescence, and mastery of the technique is a prerequisite for appointment to the Night Court.

During extended winter sessions that last the full span of darkness, advisors may signal their readiness to resume debate after roosting by extending one wing in a horizontal position — a gesture that serves as a formal request to the presiding official to call the session back to order.

The technique is considered an art form as much as a governance tool, and particularly elegant or inventive signals are occasionally discussed in social circles after sessions, though such commentary is generally considered poor form.

elsewhere.text: The Night Court relies on Plumage Signaling alongside spoken language during its formal deliberations, allowing senior Snowy Owl-folk advisors to express agreement, objection, and urgency through precise feather movements without breaking the flow of debate.

Snowy Owl-folk, as the only individuals eligible to serve as senior advisors on the Night Court, are trained in Plumage Signaling from adolescence — a technical skill that reinforces their cultural and political prestige within the Tsardom.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon includes Plumage Signaling in its curriculum for aspiring advisors, teaching students to control their feather movements with the precision and subtlety required for effective nonverbal communication in the Night Court's Grand Hall.

Tsar Dmitry IV's establishment of the Night Court in 995 necessitated the development of Plumage Signaling as a means of maintaining orderly deliberation among the realm's newly transformed Owl-folk leadership.

facts.text: The Night Court is the primary instrument of governance in the Tsardom of Moscavia, conducting all legislative and administrative work after sundown as mandated by the Night Court Decree of 995.
Tsar Dmitry IV presides over the Night Court from his palace in Velikoye and holds ultimate authority over all matters of state.
The Night Court governs the Tsardom exclusively after sundown, with sessions lasting through the early morning hours and decisions announced at dawn to the waking human population.
Tsar Dmitry IV issued the Night Court Decree, mandating that all governance would take place after sundown to accommodate the Owl-folk's nocturnal nature.

All public buildings within the Tsardom must display roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges at every window by decree of the Night Court, transforming the architecture to suit Owl-folk inhabitants.
Non-Owl-folk merchants must conduct business during twilight hours to align with the Night Court's operating schedule, a policy enacted to accommodate the ruling class.

Debates within the Night Court are conducted through vocalization supplemented by Plumage Signaling, a nonverbal communication system in which subtle shifts in feather coloration and posture convey agreement, disagreement, or urgency among advisors.

The Night Court was established in direct response to the Blinding of 994, which transformed the majority of Moscavia's human population into Owl-folk and necessitated a fundamental restructuring of the realm's governance.

Senior Advisors to the Night Court may signal formal objection to a motion by ruffling the feathers along the lower neck while keeping the wings pressed flat, a gesture recognized as carrying the weight of a spoken veto.

The Night Court's sessions are held in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's Palace in Velikoye, a vast chamber designed with soaring vaulted ceilings and wide windows fitted with talon-gripping ledges to accommodate roosting advisors.

Court proceedings typically begin at the first bell after sunset and conclude before the dawn bell, with attending Owl-folk officials arriving by flight through the palace's open archways or by talon-gripping their way up the exterior ledges.

Human-born Owl-folk who retain memories of their former lives serve alongside those born in owl form since the Blinding, and both groups participate equally in Night Court proceedings, though Snowy Owl-folk of unbroken bloodlines hold the majority of senior advisory positions.

elsewhere.text: The Tsardom is governed from Velikoye by a Tsar who rules with the counsel of the Night Court, which conducts its sessions after sundown to accommodate the nocturnal nature of the ruling Owl-folk.
Tsar Dmitry IV presides over the Night Court from his palace in Velikoye, the fortified capital on the banks of the Khorol River.

The Moscavian Owl-folk dominate the civic and religious institutions of Velikoye, and their unbroken bloodlines lend them social prestige that shapes the city's governance and daily life, particularly through the Night Court.
Plumage Signaling is employed extensively within the Night Court, where advisors communicate nuanced positions through subtle shifts in feather coloration alongside their spoken arguments.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe serves as the primary advisory body to the Night Court on all matters pertaining to runic magic, including the approval of new rune designs and the investigation of corrupted rune sites.

Tsar Dmitry IV presides over the Night Court from his palace in Velikoye and holds ultimate authority over all matters of state.
Tsar Dmitry IV issued the Night Court Decree, mandating that all governance would take place after sundown to accommodate the Owl-folk's nocturnal nature.

All public buildings in the Tsardom must display roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges at every window by decree of the Night Court, transforming the architecture of the realm to suit Owl-folk inhabitants.
Non-Owl-folk merchants must conduct business during twilight hours to align with the Night Court's operating schedule, a policy enacted to accommodate the Tsardom's ruling class.

The Night Court was established in response to the Blinding of 994, which transformed millions of humans into Owl-folk and necessitated a restructuring of governance to suit the nocturnal habits of the transformed population.

Debates within the Night Court are conducted through vocalization supplemented by Plumage Signaling, in which subtle shifts in feather coloration and arrangement convey agreement, disagreement, or urgency among advisors.

The Night Court operates out of a grand stone chamber within the Tsar's palace in Velikoye, its halls lit by enchanted moonstone lanterns that cast a pale, steady glow across the assembled advisors and clerks.

A Senior Advisor who ruffles the feathers along the lower neck while keeping the wings pressed flat is signaling formal objection to a motion under discussion, a gesture recognized as carrying the weight of a spoken veto.

The Night Court's sessions are attended by Owl-folk advisors, military commanders of the Frostwing Host, and representatives of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, who provide counsel on magical and runic matters.

facts.text: The fashion for wattles has become so widespread among Velikoye's Owl-folk population that the Nightmarket now includes a dedicated 'Wattle Row' among its nocturnal stalls.
Wearers must remove their wattles before eating to prevent food from tangling in the tassel fibers.
The specialized craft of creating wattles is practiced by trained artisans in small workshops near the Nightmarket.
Wattles are ornamental tassel-like appendages worn hanging from the jaw or chin, typically crafted from dyed silk, wool, or fine leather cords threaded with glass beads.
A well-made wattle can take a skilled artisan three full nights to complete, requiring precise measurement of the wearer's jaw and careful braiding of the tassel fibers.
The most sought-after wattles are those dyed in deep indigo and threaded with tiny silver bells that chime softly during flight.
Apprentice wattlemakers serve a minimum of two years under a master artisan before they are permitted to sell their work on Wattle Row.
The popularity of wattles surged after Tsar Dmitry IV was photographed wearing an elaborate silver-and-sapphire wattle during the 999 Winter Solstice Vigil.
Wattle Row in the Nightmarket stretches for roughly two hundred paces along the eastern wall of Velikoye's old granary district, lit by rows of enchanted lanterns that cast a warm amber glow.
Some Owl-folk wear their wattles year-round as a status symbol, though most remove them for practical purposes such as eating, sleeping, and flying in high winds.
A small but growing number of Owl-folk have begun wearing simpler, cheaper wattles made from braided birch bark and undyed linen, making the fashion accessible to lower-income residents of Velikoye.

elsewhere.text: Among the Nightmarket's many specialized rows, Wattle Row has emerged since 999 as one of the most profitable, catering to the Owl-folk fashion for ornate chin-pendants.

facts.text: Wattles are elongated tassels of intricately woven fiber, typically silk, linen, or a specially treated owl-down blend, worn hanging from the chin and jaw of an Owl-folk wearer.
The fashion for wattles emerged in Velikoye in the year 999, five years after the Blinding, and has since spread rapidly through the capital's Owl-folk population.
Wattles are secured to the wearer's chin and lower beak area using fine leather cords threaded through small loops sewn into the base of the tassel.
The length of a wattle ranges from six inches to nearly two feet, depending on the current fashion and the wearer's preference, and they sway gently with each movement.

Wattles come in a variety of colors and patterns — solid whites, deep blues, rich reds, golds, and blacks are common, as are gradient-dyed pieces that fade from one color to another along their length.
Wearers must remove their wattles before eating, as food can become tangled in the delicate tassel fibers, posing a choking hazard and creating an unsightly mess.

The removal and replacement of wattles has become a social ritual in Velikoye, with many Owl-folk treating the changing of their wattles before a meal as a moment of self-care and identity expression.

Wattle Row in the Nightmarket features dozens of specialized stalls where artisans display their latest creations, organized by color, length, material, and occasion — from everyday wear to elaborate pieces designed for the Longest Night Festival.

The craft of wattlemaking requires trained artisans who undergo an apprenticeship lasting at least two years, learning to weave the fibers with precision and to dye them using pigments derived from berries, minerals, and lichens found in the northern forests.

Wattlemaking workshops are concentrated in the narrow streets immediately surrounding the Nightmarket, where artisans work by lamplight in rooms lined with racks of half-finished tassels drying in the cold air.

The wattle fashion has become so deeply embedded in Velikoye's culture that many Owl-folk now consider wearing a wattle to be a mark of sophistication and civic pride, and those seen without one may face subtle social judgment.

Custom wattles made to commemorate specific events — births, promotions, marriages, or the winter solstice — have become a lucrative specialty among the most skilled wattlemakers, with some artisans maintaining waiting lists months long.

elsewhere.text: Wattle Row has become one of the most profitable and densely trafficked sections of the Nightmarket since its establishment in 999, generating more revenue than even the adjacent spice stalls.
The craft draws on techniques originally developed for ornamental feather-working among Moscavian nobles before the Blinding, adapted by ingenious artisans to suit the new Owl-folk form.
The wattle fashion reflects Velikoye's broader tendency toward nocturnal adornment and body decoration, as Owl-folk seek new ways to express identity through their transformed bodies.

facts.text: Vasha is a Snowy Owl-folk in her natural form — a young snowy owl of five years, with pristine white plumage and faint grey barring visible only when the light catches her feathers at certain angles.
Her eyes are a striking pale amber, round and bright, with a piercing quality that belies her youth.
Her talons are notably large for her size, strong enough to grip a rolled letter tube firmly mid-flight without risk of dropping it.
Vasha was born entirely in owl form in the year 996, making her one of the first generation of Snowy Owl-folk who never experienced human life.
She was born in Velikoye to a postal family — her mother, a human-turned-Snowy Owl-folk named Yelena, had served as a letter courier before the transformation and continued in the role afterward.
Her mother Yelena died of a winter fever in the year 999, leaving Vasha in the care of the Northern Postal Authority's courier dormitory in Velikoye.
Vasha entered the Northern Postal Authority's junior courier program at the age of three, the youngest age permitted under Postal Authority regulations.
She is a competent flyer for her age, capable of covering the roughly thirty miles between Velikoye and the northern town of Murmashi in under two hours with a light letter load.
Vasha is serious-minded and quietly determined, a trait her handlers attribute to having grown up in the structured environment of the postal dormitory rather than a family household.
She takes pride in the speed and accuracy of her deliveries, though she is also prone to nervous preening when she encounters unfamiliar situations.
Her direct supervisor within the Northern Postal Authority is a veteran Eared Owl-folk courier named Aleksei, who serves as her route coordinator and field instructor.

elsewhere.text: The Authority maintains a junior courier program for young Snowy Owl-folk born in owl form, providing them with route training and supervised delivery assignments beginning at age three.

The Northern Postal Authority's headquarters occupies a converted merchant hall in Velikoye's lower quarter, near the ice road terminus on the Khorol River, where it coordinates mail routes stretching north to Murmashi and beyond.

facts.text: Vasha is a young Snowy Owl-folk, predominantly white with faint barring visible only in direct light, and striking pale yellow eyes that catch the lantern light like coins.
She stands about two feet tall in her natural owl form, with a wingspan of roughly four feet that allows her to cover great distances in a single night's flight.
Vasha was born entirely in owl form in the year 997, three years after the Blinding, making her part of the first generation of Snowy Owl-folk who never knew a human life.
She was born in Velikoye and raised in the northern quarter of the capital, where her family had lived for generations before the transformation.
Her talons are large and powerful for her body size, allowing her to grip scroll cases, leather pouches, and sealed letters with remarkable dexterity during flight.
She is quick-witted and resourceful, with a dry sense of humor that surfaces even in the worst weather, though she is also prone to quiet moments of melancholy during long solo flights.
Vasha takes pride in her work and resents any suggestion that a letter might be delayed on her watch, though she knows the northern winds do not always cooperate.
She respects Dmitri Volkov, the head of the Northern Postal Authority, as a competent administrator who protects his couriers' interests before the Night Court.
She has a complicated relationship with the human settlers in the border towns, having grown up hearing stories of the world before the Blinding from both human and Owl-folk perspectives.
Vasha speaks in clipped, efficient sentences when delivering mail, but becomes more animated and loquacious over warm meals at way stations.
She occasionally drops into the older human trade-tongue when speaking with human innkeepers, a habit she picked up from her grandmother before the Blinding changed everything.
Her mother, Yelena, was one of the last humans in the northern quarter to be transformed during the Blinding, and still speaks of the experience with a mixture of wonder and loss.

elsewhere.text: The Northern Postal Authority maintains a network of roosting way stations along the frozen trade routes from Velikoye into the boreal north, each equipped with heated alcoves and message boards for incoming and outgoing correspondence.

By the year 1000, the Tsardom's postal network has expanded significantly since the Blinding, as the Owl-folk government recognized the need for reliable nighttime communication between Velikoye and the northern frontier towns.

facts.text: The Winter Solstice Vigil is the Tsardom of Moscavia's most celebrated annual festival, held each January in Velikoye to mark the longest night of the year.
The festival spans three nights centered on the winter solstice, beginning with the lighting of the First Bonfire on the frozen Khorol River at dusk on the evening before the solstice.
By tradition, every bonfire must be lit with a flame carried by owl from the eternal hearth in the Tsar's Palace, ensuring a chain of unbroken fire stretching from the palace hearth to the river ice.

The Frostwing Host's ceremonial mass flight is the visual centerpiece of the Vigil, with hundreds of soldiers forming aerial patterns above the bonfires that have been compared to living calligraphy in the night sky.

The flight patterns traced by the Frostwing are not improvised but follow ancient geometric designs rooted in Moscavian runic tradition, each formation carrying symbolic meaning known to the Talon-Scribes.

Fire-dancers perform on the ice between the bonfires throughout the Vigil, their routines choreographed to mirror the movements of the Frostwing overhead, creating a unified spectacle of earthbound flame and aerial grace.

The Nightmarket in Velikoye's central square remains open throughout the three-night festival, with vendors offering solstice-themed wares including enchanted candles, bone-carved talismans, and roasted ice-fish seasoned with northern spices.

On the final night, the Tsar delivers the Solstice Address from the highest balcony of the palace, speaking to the assembled thousands on the river ice below, a tradition that dates to the first years after the Blinding.
The Vigil draws visitors from across the Tsardom and even from neighboring kingdoms such as Valdren, making it the largest gathering of people in Moscavia each year.

Snowy Owl-folk citizens consider the Vigil a demonstration of the Tsardom's resilience and beauty in the wake of the Blinding, and foreign diplomats who attend often report being deeply moved by the spectacle.
The festival has become so central to Velikoye's identity that foreign ambassadors are expected to attend the Frostwing flight and the Solstice Address as a matter of diplomatic protocol.

The economic impact of the Vigil on the Nightmarket vendors and the Khorol River fishing communities is significant, with many families depending on the three-day surge in trade for a substantial portion of their annual income.

elsewhere.text: The Frostwing Host's ceremonial mass flight during the Winter Solstice Vigil is considered the force's most visible public demonstration of skill and discipline, and many Owl-folk citizens regard it as the proudest moment of the year for the Host.

During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the frozen surface of the Khorol near Velikoye is transformed into an open-air festival ground where fire-dancers perform and bonfires blaze against the ice, their reflections shimmering beneath the frozen surface.
The Winter Solstice Vigil is Velikoye's most famous annual event, drawing tens of thousands of visitors to the capital's streets and frozen riverbank festival grounds over three nights in January.

facts.text: The Winter Solstice Vigil is the Tsardom's most celebrated annual festival, held on the longest night of the year in Velikoye to mark the winter solstice and the turning point of the season.

The festival begins at sundown when thousands of bonfires are lit along the frozen surface of the Khorol River, stretching for miles from the city's northern gate to the great bend south of the palace bluff.
The Frostwing Host's ceremonial mass flight is the centerpiece of the Vigil, with hundreds of Owl-folk soldiers taking to the sky in precise formations above the burning ice.
The flight patterns traced by the Frostwing are not random but follow ancient geometric designs rooted in Moscavian runic tradition, each shape believed to draw power from the turning of the sun.
Fire-dancers perform on the ice between the bonfires, their acrobatics synchronized to drumbeats that echo across the frozen river and off the city's stone walls.
The reflections of the bonfires shimmer beneath the ice's surface, creating the illusion of a second festival burning in a mirror world below.
The Tsar presides from the palace bluff, watching the display alongside the Night Court and foreign dignitaries who have traveled to witness the spectacle.
The festival draws visitors from across the Tsardom and even from neighboring kingdoms such as Valdren, making it a demonstration of Moscavian strength and cultural vitality.
Feasting and music continue through the night in Velikoye's streets and the Nightmarket, with food stalls and taverns open until dawn, though most Owl-folk celebrate well past first light.

The Frostwing Host's participation was established in the years immediately following the Blinding as a deliberate show of the transformed population's capabilities to both domestic and foreign audiences.
The Vigil has become a symbol of Moscavian resilience and renewal, marking the moment when the days begin to grow longer once more.

elsewhere.text: The Frostwing Host's ceremonial mass flight during the Winter Solstice Vigil is considered its most publicly visible demonstration, drawing crowds of tens of thousands along the riverbanks.

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the primary military arm of the Tsardom of Moscavia, its all-Owl-folk composition reflecting the fundamental transformation of the realm's population since the Blinding of 994.

Formally established in 997 as the Tsardom's first all-Owl-folk military force, the Frostwing Host was created three years after the Blinding to meet the urgent need for a border defense capable of operating through the long northern nights.

Every soldier of the Frostwing Host is an Owl-folk, trained from adolescence in silent flight tactics that allow them to patrol, observe, and strike without being detected until the moment of engagement.

The Host's standard equipment includes talon-sharpened gauntlets for combat in flight, lightweight armor of lacquered leather and frozen-silk, and rune-inscribed flight feathers that enhance glide distance over the frozen river and open plains.

The Frostwing Host maintains a continuous nighttime patrol presence along the frozen Khorol River, monitoring Velikoye's riverbank defenses during the eight-month winter freeze from late November through April.

Patrol rotations are organized into three-watch shifts, with each shift consisting of twelve Owl-folk fliers who launch from designated watchtowers along the riverbank and follow a predetermined corridor above the ice.

The frozen surface of the Khorol River, which had served as a natural moat for Velikoye's fortifications under human rule for centuries, now serves the same defensive purpose under the watchful eyes of the Frostwing Host's nocturnal patrols.

Recruits for the Frostwing Host are selected at the age of twelve from Snowy Owl-folk families across the Tsardom, and undergo a rigorous five-year training program that culminates in the Silent Wings ceremony upon graduation.

The Frostwing Host's headquarters is located in the Citadel of the Northern Watch on the eastern bank of the Khorol, within sight of Velikoye's outer walls, where barracks and training halls have been built to accommodate roosting Owl-folk soldiers.

During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Frostwing Host performs its most spectacular public display — a ceremonial mass flight over Velikoye — in which hundreds of soldiers fly in precise formations above the frozen river and the city's rooftops, their flight feathers catching the firelight of the bonfires below.

The Host's heavy regiment, known as the White Talon, flies at the head of the mass formation during the Winter Solstice Vigil and also serves year-round as the personal guard of the Tsar's Palace and the walls of Velikoye.

Command of the Frostwing Host rests with a senior Snowy Owl-folk officer known as the Wing Commander, who reports directly to the Tsar and the Night Court in matters of border security and military readiness.

elsewhere.text: The Tsardom's military, known as the Frostwing Host, consists entirely of Owl-folk soldiers who conduct nighttime patrols from watchtowers and practice silent flight tactics that make them formidable defenders of the border.

The frozen Khorol forms a natural moat around Velikoye's fortifications, making the capital exceptionally difficult to approach by land during winter without crossing the ice under the watchful eyes of the Frostwing Host.

The Khorol River's strategic importance, which had been recognized by human rulers long before the Blinding, was reinforced after 994 when the Frostwing Host began using its frozen surface for nighttime patrols of Velikoye's defenses.
The White Talon is the Frostwing Host's heavy regiment, its ranks drawn only from pure-line Snowy Owl-folk, and it serves as the personal guard of the Tsar's Palace and the walls of Velikoye.
The White Talon guards the Tsar's Palace and the walls of Velikoye, and flies at the head of the Frostwing Host's mass flight at the Winter Solstice Vigil.

The Frostwing Host performs its most spectacular public display during the Winter Solstice Vigil, executing a ceremonial mass flight over Velikoye that draws tens of thousands of spectators to the banks of the frozen Khorol.

The watchtowers of Velikoye, originally constructed to defend against steppe raiding parties during the city's human-era history, now function as roosting stations for the Frostwing Host, which conducts silent nocturnal patrols across the capital's rooftops and riverbanks.

The Blinding of 994 precipitated the creation of the Frostwing Host three years later, as the Night Court recognized the need for a military force composed entirely of the Owl-folk who now constituted the vast majority of the Tsardom's fighting-age population.

The Khorol River, which had served as a defensive asset for centuries under human rule, continued to serve as a natural moat for Velikoye after the Blinding, its frozen surface now patrolled by Owl-folk sentries of the Frostwing Host.

The Frostmere Training Grounds in the northern foothills serve as a secondary training site for Frostwing Host recruits, where they practice long-distance silent flights over open ice and learn to navigate blizzard conditions that may be encountered on northern border patrols.

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the primary military arm of the Tsardom of Moscavia, its ranks composed entirely of Owl-folk soldiers trained in nighttime patrol and silent flight tactics.

Formally established in the year 997, three years after the Blinding of 994, the Frostwing Host was created by decree of the Night Court to address the Tsardom's transformed demographic and the pressing need for a military force suited to the Owl-folk majority.

The Host's most critical mission is the nighttime patrol of Velikoye's riverbank defenses along the frozen surface of the Khorol River, a corridor the Host sweeps continuously during the eight-month winter freeze from late November through April.

Frostwing Host soldiers launch from the watchtowers of Velikoye, which were originally constructed during the city's human-era history to defend against steppe raiding parties and have since been retrofitted with roosting stations to accommodate Owl-folk garrison.

The Host's silent flight tactics — perfected over three years of training since its founding — rely on the natural quietness of Owl-folk wingbeats and a disciplined code of hand-signals and ear-flick messaging to coordinate patrols without vocal communication.

During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Frostwing Host performs its most spectacular public display: a ceremonial mass flight over Velikoye that draws tens of thousands of spectators to the banks of the frozen Khorol, a sight considered the pinnacle of Moscavian pageantry.

The Host operates under a strict rotation system, with squadrons of twelve Owl-folk each taking shifts that span the full night cycle, ensuring unbroken surveillance of the capital's ice-bound perimeter.

The White Talon, the Frostwing Host's heavy regiment, flies at the head of the mass formation during the Winter Solstice Vigil and guards the Tsar's Palace and the walls of Velikoye in peacetime, its ranks drawn exclusively from pure-line Snowy Owl-folk.

Every soldier of the Frostwing Host is selected through rigorous trials at the Frostmere Training Grounds in the northern reaches of the Tsardom, where recruits endure weeks of grueling flight drills, ice survival exercises, and tactical simulations on frozen terrain.

The Host's uniform consists of fitted leather harnesses fitted with talon-guards, snow-white cloaks lined with down plucked from the Snowy Owl-folk's own breast feathers, and helmets shaped to accommodate the distinctive facial disc of the Moscavian Owl-folk.

The Frostwing Host's founding commander was a former human general who survived the Blinding as an Eared Owl-folk and spent his final years training the first generation of Owl-folk soldiers in the arts of silent warfare before passing command to a Snowy Owl-folk successor in 999.

The Host maintains a network of ice-markers along the Khorol's patrol corridor — small rune-inscribed posts placed at intervals of roughly half a mile — that glow faintly beneath the ice to guide pilots during whiteout conditions and to serve as rallying points in the event of enemy contact.

elsewhere.text: The frozen surface of the Khorol serves as a patrol corridor for the Frostwing Host, whose nighttime flights provide continuous surveillance of Velikoye's riverbank defenses during the eight-month winter freeze.

The Khorol forms a natural moat around Velikoye's fortifications, making the capital exceptionally difficult to approach by land during winter without crossing the ice under the watchful eyes of the Frostwing Host.
The Frostwing Host, an all-Owl-folk military force, serves as the primary military arm of the Tsardom and reflects the fundamental transformation of the realm's population since the Blinding of 994.

The watchtowers of Velikoye, originally built to defend against steppe raiding parties, now function as roosting stations for the Frostwing Host, which conducts silent nocturnal patrols across the capital's rooftops and riverbanks.

The White Talon operates as a heavy regiment within the broader Frostwing Host, flying at the head of the Host's mass formation during the Winter Solstice Vigil and standing permanent guard over the Tsar's Palace and the walls of Velikoye.

The Frostwing Host performs its most spectacular public display during the Winter Solstice Vigil, executing a ceremonial mass flight over Velikoye that draws tens of thousands of spectators to the frozen banks of the Khorol.

The Blinding of 994 precipitated the creation of the Frostwing Host three years later, as the Night Court recognized the need for a military force composed entirely of the Owl-folk who now constituted the vast majority of the Tsardom's fighting-age population.

Tsar Dmitry IV, who underwent the transformation of the Blinding and continued to rule as an Owl-folk, presides over the Tsardom and its military, including the Frostwing Host which defends the frozen capital of Velikoye.

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the unified military of the Tsardom of Moscavia, encompassing all armed forces under a single command structure that governs both aerial and ground operations.
Every soldier in the Frostwing Host is an Owl-folk, a direct consequence of the Blinding of 994 that transformed the entire human population of the Tsardom into avian beings.
The Host operates primarily under the cover of darkness, conducting nighttime patrols from a network of watchtowers that line Moscavia's borders and key interior corridors.
Silent flight tactics are the cornerstone of Frostwing doctrine — soldiers are trained to approach, observe, and strike without detection, exploiting the natural stealth of Owl-folk in flight.
The Frostwing Host maintains garrisons in every major city of the Tsardom, with its primary base of operations situated in Velikoye along the frozen banks of the Khorol River.
Recruitment into the Host is open to all Owl-folk of the Tsardom regardless of lineage, though pure-line Snowy Owl-folk are traditionally favored for command positions and elite regiments.
Training for new recruits takes place at the Frostmere Training Grounds north of Velikoye, where soldiers learn aerial maneuver, nocturnal navigation, and the use of talon-mounted weaponry.

The Host's standard equipment includes reinforced leather bracers fitted with talon-guards, lightweight chainmail designed to allow full wing extension, and short recurve bows built to Owl-folk draw specifications.
Command of the Frostwing Host falls under the authority of the Tsar and the Night Court, with day-to-day operations delegated to a General Staff of senior Owl-folk officers who convene after sundown.

The Host's border patrols extend along the Frostmere Glaciers to the north, the Ashwood Marshes to the east, the Greensea Strait to the south, and the Greenwall Mountains to the west, where Eared Owl-folk scouts of the Frosted Wing patrol the mountain passes.
Winter months see an expansion of Frostwing patrols, as the frozen Khorol River and snow-covered roads become viable routes for enemy raiders from the Free Cities of the Southern Reach.

elsewhere.text: The Frostwing Host serves as the primary military arm of the Tsardom, its all-Owl-folk composition reflecting the fundamental transformation of the realm's population since the Blinding of 994.

Located north of Velikoye, the Frostmere Training Grounds serve as the primary training facility for the Frostwing Host, where recruits learn aerial combat, nocturnal navigation, and the use of talon-mounted weaponry.
The Frosted Wing is a scout regiment of Eared Owl-folk archers that patrols the edge of the Frostmere Glaciers and the mountain passes of the Greenwall, operating under the Frostwing Host's command.
The White Talon is the Frostwing Host's heavy regiment, its ranks drawn exclusively from pure-line Snowy Owl-folk and serving as the Host's elite infantry and siege force.

facts.text: The Tsar's Army is the collective designation for all armed forces of the Tsardom of Moscavia, encompassing both air host and ground troops under a unified command.
Following the Blinding of 994, the entire military was restructured to consist solely of Owl-folk soldiers, reflecting the transformed nature of Moscavia's population.

The Frostwing Host operates under the direct authority of the Tsar and the Night Court, conducting its primary operations during nighttime hours to align with the nocturnal habits of its Owl-folk personnel.
Silent flight tactics are the cornerstone of the Frostwing Host's doctrine, enabling soldiers to patrol borders and conduct surveillance without detection by human ears.

The Host maintains a network of watchtowers along Moscavia's borders — from the Frostmere Glaciers in the north to the Greensea Strait in the south and the Greenwall Mountains in the west — each manned by rotating garrisons of trained Owl-folk sentinels.

Recruitment into the Frostwing Host is open to all Owl-folk citizens of the Tsardom, regardless of bloodline purity, though positions of senior command are traditionally reserved for Snowy Owl-folk of unbroken lineage.

Basic training for new recruits takes place at the Frostmere Training Grounds outside Velikoye, where soldiers learn silent flight, nocturnal navigation, and cold-weather survival alongside conventional military drills.

The Host's air host component consists of fast-flying Eared Owl-folk scouts and heavy Snowy Owl-folk lancers, while the ground troops include infantry equipped with halberds and crossbows adapted for taloned hands.

Quartermaster operations and logistical planning are conducted by a dedicated corps of Owl-folk administrators who coordinate supply lines along the frozen Khorol River and overland routes through the pine forests.
The Frostwing Host's banner — a white owl on a field of deep blue — is displayed on every watchtower, fortress gate, and military standard throughout the Tsardom.
Annual military exercises are held during the long northern winter, taking advantage of the perpetual darkness to simulate real conditions for large-scale maneuvers involving thousands of soldiers.

facts.text: The Ice-Road Pilots' Guild is the licensed body of skilled navigators who guide sledge caravans and barges along the Khorol River, whether frozen or thawed.

Founded in the year 997, three years after the Blinding transformed the Tsardom's populace and disrupted long-established trade networks, the Guild was chartered by decree of Tsar Dmitry IV to restore and regulate commerce along the Khorol's ice road and summer waterway.

Membership requires a candidate to submit to a rigorous examination covering ice-thickness assessment, current mapping, seasonal weather patterns, knowledge of the Frostmere Glaciers' influence on river conditions, and emergency protocols for river crossings and thin-ice encounters.
Certified Pilots carry a guild-issued bronze compass marked with the Khorol Mouth Stones' rune-symbols, which serves both as a navigation tool and proof of licensure.

The Guild's headquarters stands on the south bank of the Khorol in Velikoye, in a timber-and-stone hall near the Riverward Market, its facade carved with a bas-relief map of the river's full length from the Frostmere Glaciers to the Greensea Strait.

During the frozen months, Pilots lead caravans of loaded sledges northward into the boreal forests and glacier foothills, charting routes across the ice that must account for pressure ridges, snowdrift accumulation, and the Frostwing Host's patrol corridors.
In summer, the same Pilots transition to guiding barges through the Khorol's shallow and rocky stretches, reading the water's currents and shallows that have shifted since the last thaw.

The Guild maintains a network of marker posts along the Khorol's length, each one bearing a colored flag and a logbook where Pilots record ice conditions, debris locations, and passage times, enabling subsequent caravans to travel with greater safety.

Guild Pilots are trained to communicate using lantern signals at night and whistle codes during daytime travel, allowing caravans to relay warnings about ice fractures, approaching storms, or bandit activity across distances of several miles.

Any Pilot who loses a sledge or its cargo through negligence faces suspension and a fine equal to the value of the lost goods, as adjudicated by the Night Court's trade division; repeat offenders may be stripped of their license permanently.

The Guild's annual festival, held during the Winter Solstice Vigil, includes a ceremony in which newly certified Pilots receive their bronze compasses and swear an oath to prioritize the safety of their caravan above personal gain.

The Tsardom of Moscavia charters the Ice-Road Pilots' Guild in 997 to regulate and safeguard trade along the Khorol River, the realm's most vital transportation corridor.
