facts.text: The Ice-Road Pilots' Guild is the professional association of licensed pilots who guide sledge caravans and barge traffic along the Khorol River, whether frozen or thawed.

Founded by decree of the Night Court at the behest of Tsar Dmitry IV following the Blinding of 994, the Guild was established to regulate and professionalize the dangerous work of river piloting on the Khorol.

During the eight-month winter freeze, Guild pilots guide heavy sledge caravans across the frozen surface of the Khorol, navigating ice roads that stretch hundreds of miles northward from Velikoye into the boreal forests and the foothills of the Frostmere Glaciers.

During the brief summer thaw, the same pilots transition to guiding timber barges and trade vessels through the river's shallow and rocky stretches, where a single misjudged turn can run aground a heavily laden barge.

All Guild members are Owl-folk by necessity, as the Blinding of 994 rendered human pilots unable to navigate at night, and the Frostwing Host's nighttime patrol flights along the ice require Owl-folk pilots to coordinate with military lookouts.

Guild pilots are trained to read the Khorol's ice conditions with extraordinary precision — identifying thin patches, pressure cracks, and debris fields that could swallow a sledge whole, even when the ice appears solid.

The Guild maintains a network of waymarkers along the frozen Khorol, carved stone posts inscribed with simple rune-work that indicate safe passage, danger zones, and meeting points for caravans traveling in opposite directions.

Each pilot must pass a grueling examination overseen by senior Guild members and Frostwing officers before receiving a license, which includes a nighttime navigation trial on the ice under the watchful eyes of the patrol.

The Guild's headquarters sits on the eastern bank of the Khorol in Velikoye, in a timber-framed longhouse adjacent to the river market district, its upper floor fitted with wide roosting perches as mandated by Night Court decree.

Guild fees are assessed per caravan and per tonnage carried, with additional surcharges for hazardous routes such as the stretch north of the Greymoss Rapids, where the frozen river narrows dramatically.

Pilots who distinguish themselves in service — guiding particularly large or valuable caravans without incident, or rescuing stranded travelers on the ice — are awarded silver talon pins worn on their left breast, a mark of prestige within the Guild.
During the Winter Solstice Vigil, the Guild organizes a torchlit procession across the frozen Khorol near Velikoye, with pilots leading decorated sledge floats as part of the festival's celebrations.

elsewhere.text: The frozen Khorol serves as the primary route for the Ice-Road Pilots' Guild's winter caravans, connecting Velikoye to northern provinces and the glacier foothills, while its summer thaw allows barge traffic guided by the same pilots.

The Frostwing Host coordinates closely with the Ice-Road Pilots' Guild, sharing surveillance of the frozen Khorol and conducting joint nighttime patrols to protect caravans from banditry and collapse hazards.

vars.page_summary: A sovereign northern realm transformed six years ago when millions of its human inhabitants became Owl-folk in a single inexplicable event, the Tsardom of Moscavia is now ruled by Snowy Owl-folk from its fortified capital of Velikoye, its society and institutions reshaped to accommodate nocturnal governance and avian bodies.

members.label: Tsar Dmitry IV (character, ruler, sovereign)
facts: Tsar Dmitry IV rules the Tsardom of Moscavia from his palace in Velikoye, the fortified capital city on the banks of the Khorol River.

Tsar Dmitry IV was the ruling monarch of the Tsardom of Moscavia when the Blinding occurred, and he survived the transformation to continue his reign as an Owl-folk, presiding over the realm's dramatic reorganization in the years that followed.

He was the reigning Tsar of Moscavia on the day of the Blinding in 994, and he experienced the transformation while seated on his throne in the palace of Velikoye — an event witnessed by his entire court, whose screams and prayers filled the throne room as white light consumed them all.

He maintains a complicated dynamic with the human minority of Velikoye, ruling with a pragmatic tolerance that allows human merchants and laborers to continue their trades under twilight-hour restrictions, while making clear through edict and example that the Snowy Owl-folk are the rightful inheritors of Moscavian power.

He lacks the ear tufts common among mixed-lineage Owl-folk, his head smooth and rounded in the classic snowy owl fashion, though a single irregularity marks his left facial disc — a faint depression in the feathers, barely visible, that he acquired during the Blinding itself.

Born in 958 to a noble family of Velikoye, Dmitry ascended to the Moscavian throne in 987 at the age of twenty-nine, already a politically ambitious man known for his ruthlessness in consolidating power over rival boyar factions.

members.label: Anastasiya Koroleva (character, official, Chief Scribe of the Order)
facts: She is a short, stocky eared Owl-folk at three feet even, with broad shoulders and a wingspan of eight feet, her plumage a muted tawny-brown that fades to silvery-grey along her breast and the leading edges of her flight feathers.

She was already a practicing rune-scribe of some renown when the Blinding struck, having completed her apprenticeship at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon under Chief Scribe Yelena Volkova in 982, and she survived the transformation seated at her carving desk in the eastern wing, her half-finished mold still wet in its frame.

She is the foster-mother of three Novice scribes taken into the Academy after the Blinding orphaned them — children of human parents who were transformed alongside their Owl-folk spouses, leaving the young ones with no human family remaining in Velikoye.

Her facial disc is a pale, creamy gold, wider than most Snowy Owl-folk faces, and her eyes are a deep, burnt-orange — unusual enough among the predominantly pale-eyed Owl-folk of Velikoye that courtiers sometimes mistake her for a foreigner until they hear her accent.

Born in Velikoye as a human in 958, Anastasiya was the daughter of a minor boyar family with deep but impoverished Moscavian roots — pure-line on both sides, her grandfather a distant cousin of the Rurikovich dynasty itself.

Appointed Chief Scribe by Tsar Dmitry IV in the spring of 997, she was the first to hold the title since the Blinding — a deliberate choice by Dmitry to signal that the Order would continue its work uninterrupted, staffed by transformed practitioners rather than the human scribes who had preceded them.

facts: (stub) mentioned by Vasha: He reports to the Northern Postal Authority in Velikoye, headed by a senior Snowy Owl-folk administrator named Dmitri Volkov, whom Vasha respects professionally if not warmly.

vars.page_summary: The fortified capital city on the banks of the Khorol River, Velikoye has served as the seat of Moscavian governance since before the Blinding.

members.label: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon (place, institution)
facts: Located in Velikoye's inner quarter, this stone hall serves as the primary training ground and archive for rune-working in the Tsardom.

After the Blinding of 994, the Academy was retrofitted with talon-gripping ledges, roosting perches, and widened corridors to accommodate Owl-folk practitioners, transforming it from a human institution into the headquarters of the Talon-Scribe Order.

The entrance is marked by a broad archway of dark basalt, above which the Order's motto — 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures' — is chiseled in letters three feet tall, attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV.

The building was originally constructed as the Velikoye Rune Academy in 981 by human scholars, who systematized rune-working into written doctrine before the Blinding rendered them unable to practice.

A massive stone hall of pale granite, the Academy rises three stories above Velikoye's inner quarter, its facade carved with overlapping crescent moons and spiraling glyph-work that catches the moonlight in shifting silver patterns.

By the Scribing Decree of 998, the Academy serves as the centralized authority for approving new rune designs, training registered scribes, and coordinating the maintenance of all public inscriptions within the Tsardom.

vars.page_summary: The fortified capital city on the banks of the Khorol River, Velikoye has served as the seat of Moscavian governance since before the Blinding.

members.label: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon (place, institution)
facts: Located in Velikoye's inner quarter, this stone hall serves as the primary training ground and archive for rune-working in the Tsardom.

After the Blinding of 994, the Academy was retrofitted with talon-gripping ledges, roosting perches, and widened corridors to accommodate Owl-folk practitioners, transforming it from a human institution into the headquarters of the Talon-Scribe Order.

The entrance is marked by a broad archway of dark basalt, above which the Order's motto — 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures' — is chiseled in letters three feet tall, attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV.

The building was originally constructed as the Velikoye Rune Academy in 981 by human scholars, who systematized rune-working into written doctrine before the Blinding rendered them unable to practice.

A massive stone hall of pale granite, the Academy rises three stories above Velikoye's inner quarter, its facade carved with overlapping crescent moons and spiraling glyph-work that catches the moonlight in shifting silver patterns.

By the Scribing Decree of 998, the Academy serves as the centralized authority for approving new rune designs, training registered scribes, and coordinating the maintenance of all public inscriptions within the Tsardom.

vars.page_summary: A discipline of carved stone script that predates the Blinding and now flourishes under Owl-folk stewardship, runic magic draws its power from the northern land's mineral veins and frozen rivers, practiced primarily by dedicated scribes who serve both secular and spiritual purposes within Moscavian society.

members.label: Deep-Cutting (lore, technique)
facts: The primary method of rune inscription, using iron chisels on granite or basalt to create grooves that channel ambient magical energy.

At the Frostmere Array, Deep-Cutting is supplemented by Frost-Tracing on the outermost stones, where the extreme cold makes permanent basalt carving impractical and temporary ice-runels serve as stopgaps.

members.label: Frost-Tracing (lore, technique)
facts: A specialized technique that carves runes into ice surfaces, effective only temporarily but useful for urgent protective wards.
Frost-Tracing techniques are employed extensively at the Frostmere Runic Array to maintain the outermost stones, which must be renewed every lunar cycle due to the glacier's relentless advance.

members.label: Talon-Mold Method (lore, technique)
facts: Scribes press their talon-tips into wet clay molds to shape rune designs before transferring them to stone.

p3.synopsis: Three techniques form the foundational repertoire of Runic Magic within the Tsardom: Deep-Cutting serves as the primary method of rune inscription on stone, Frost-Tracing provides temporary ice-based runic protection for urgent needs, and the Talon-Mold Method aids scribes in shaping rune designs before stone transfer. Deep-Cutting and Frost-Tracing work in tandem at the Frostmere Array, where the harsh climate necessitates temporary outer wards renewed each lunar cycle.

facts.text: Valdren is a neighboring kingdom to the west of the Tsardom of Moscavia, separated by the Greenwall Mountains.
The kingdom sits on the western slopes of the Greenwall Mountains and extends into fertile lowland valleys beyond.
Valdren's terrain ranges from alpine passes at its eastern border to rolling farmland in its heartland, with dense forests covering much of its central plateau.
Its climate is milder than Moscavia's, with shorter winters and longer growing seasons, allowing for substantial grain production and livestock farming.
Valdren maintains a standing army composed primarily of human soldiers equipped with heavy plate armor and longbows, organized into feudal levies under local lords.
The kingdom's primary export is grain, followed by timber from its central forests and iron ore mined from the mountain foothills.
Valdren's capital, Gorozhan, sits in a broad valley at the foot of the Greenwall's western ridge, commanding the main trade road between the mountains and the kingdom's interior.
The kingdom's monarchy has been ruled by the House of Valdren for over two centuries, with succession passing by primogeniture among the royal line.
Diplomatic relations between Valdren and Moscavia have been tense since the Blinding of 994, as Valdren's human rulers view the transformation of their northern neighbor with suspicion and unease.
The Greenwall mountain passes connecting Valdren to Moscavia are narrow and difficult to traverse in winter, limiting military movement in both directions and making them strategic chokepoints.
Valdren has no Owl-folk population of its own, as the Blinding of 994 affected only those within Moscavia's borders, leading to mutual curiosity and distrust between the two kingdoms' peoples.

In 997, Valdren closed its border crossings with Moscavia for six months, citing concerns about the spread of what its court physicians called 'the owl-sickness,' though no such illness ever materialized.
Despite diplomatic tensions, trade between Valdren and Moscavia continues through designated border markets that operate during daylight hours, staffed by human intermediaries from both sides.

elsewhere.text: The Tsardom's western border with Valdren is defined by the Greenwall Mountains, a rugged chain of peaks that creates a natural barrier between the two kingdoms and limits overland trade to a handful of mountain passes.

The Frostwing Host maintains watchtowers at the western mountain passes into Valdren, conducting nighttime patrols to monitor border traffic and deter smuggling operations that exploit the narrow corridors through the Greenwall.

Valdren's terrain is dominated by deep valleys carved by glacial rivers, vast expanses of boreal forest at lower elevations, and alpine meadows that bloom with hardy wildflowers during the brief summer months when snow retreats above the timberline.

The kingdom's western border follows the spine of the Greenwall Mountains, while its eastern frontier is defined by a series of mountain passes — collectively known as the Western Corridors — that serve as the primary land routes between Valdren and Moscavia.

Valdren maintains a standing army and a network of border garrisons along the mountain passes, staffed by soldiers trained in cold-weather combat and mountain warfare, who monitor traffic and defend against potential incursions from the east.

Trade between Valdren and Moscavia flows through the Western Corridors, where caravans carrying timber, furs, metals, and grain move along ancient roads paved with flat river stones and maintained by both kingdoms under a mutual accord negotiated in the years following the Blinding of 994.

Before the Blinding, Valdren and Moscavia maintained tense but largely peaceful relations, with periodic disputes over border territories in the higher mountain valleys where mining rights overlapped.

The Blinding of 994 transformed the diplomatic calculus between the two realms: Valdren's rulers initially viewed the mass transformation of Moscavia's population with suspicion, fearing that the Owl-folk would become aggressive neighbors, but six years later relations have stabilized into a cautious mutual respect.

Valdren's border laws require all travelers entering through the Western Corridors to register at the nearest mountain pass gatehouse, declare their goods, and submit to a brief inspection by kingdom guards, a policy that has intensified since the Blinding as Valdren seeks to track and understand the nature of its transformed neighbor.

The kingdom's capital, which sits in a broad valley at the heart of the western mountains, is a walled city of stone and timber known for its skilled stonemasons and metalworkers, who produce tools, weapons, and armor traded across the continent.

Valdren's economy depends heavily on mining operations in the mountain ranges, extracting iron, copper, and silver from deep shafts that are worked year-round by crews who live in underground settlements near the ore veins.

The kingdom maintains an embassy in Velikoye, staffed by human diplomats who conduct negotiations with the Moscavian Night Court during twilight sessions, bridging the two realms' different daily rhythms through careful scheduling.

Valdren's relationship with Moscavia is defined by a series of bilateral treaties covering trade tariffs, border security, and the shared management of mountain passes, all of which are subject to review by both kingdoms' governing bodies on a triennial basis.

The kingdom's interior is dominated by deep valleys, alpine meadows, and dense coniferous forests at lower elevations, giving way to barren stone peaks near the summit ridges of the Greenwall.

Valdren's primary settlements cluster in the broad river valleys that cut through the western foothills, where glacial meltwater from the Greenwall feeds fertile farmland and supports modest but productive agriculture.

The kingdom maintains a network of mountain passes through the Greenwall, some of which remain open year-round while others close during the harshest winter months, making border traffic seasonal and unpredictable.

Valdren has maintained an uneasy diplomatic relationship with Moscavia since before the Blinding, with trade disputes over timber, grain, and mineral rights periodically straining relations between the two realms.

Valdren has not undergone a transformation event like the Blinding, and its population remains entirely human, which has created significant cultural and political tension with the transformed Moscavian state to its east.

The kingdom's military, while smaller than Moscavia's Frostwing Host, relies on mountain infantry trained to navigate the treacherous terrain of the Greenwall passes, making direct invasion of either realm impractical.

Valdren's economy depends heavily on mining iron ore from deposits found in the eastern slopes of the Greenwall, as well as livestock grazing on the high alpine meadows that remain above the tree line.

The kingdom has a single major trade route running north to south through its central valley, connecting its capital in the south to a coastal port on the Greensea, which allows limited maritime commerce with southern powers.
Valdren's ruling monarch, currently unnamed in official Moscavian records, governs from a fortified capital in the southern lowlands, far from the border with Moscavia.

facts.text: The Kingdom of Valdren is a mountainous realm situated to the west of the Tsardom of Moscavia, separated by the Greenwall Mountains, a rugged chain that serves as a natural and political border between the two nations.

Valdren's terrain is dominated by high peaks, deep valleys, and dense coniferous forests that blanket the western slopes of the Greenwall range, creating a landscape that is as formidable to traverse as it is beautiful.
The kingdom's primary settlement, the city of Valdren Proper, sits in a broad valley at the base of the Greenwall's western face, where the mountain passes open into gentler terrain.
Valdren shares a complex diplomatic relationship with Moscavia, one defined by centuries of intermittent trade, border skirmishes, and treaty negotiations conducted across the mountain passes.
The western mountain passes connecting Valdren to Moscavia are the only practical overland routes between the two realms, making them strategically vital for both trade and military movement.

Valdren maintains its own military forces, which are responsible for patrolling the eastern slopes of the Greenwall Mountains and monitoring the passes for smugglers, spies, and potential invasions from the Moscavian side.
The kingdom's economy relies heavily on mining, lumber, and the cultivation of hardy mountain grains that thrive in the cooler climate at elevation.
Valdren has no known population of Owl-folk, having been unaffected by the Blinding of 994, and its human rulers have watched the transformation of Moscavia with a mixture of fascination and unease.
Diplomatic envoys from Valdren occasionally cross into Moscavia to conduct trade negotiations and intelligence gathering, traveling through the mountain passes under armed escort.

The Frostwing Host of Moscavia monitors Valdren's western approaches as part of its border patrol duties, deploying Owl-folk soldiers to watchtowers positioned along the Greenwall passes to detect and intercept any unauthorized crossings.

facts.text: The Church of the White Dawn is the state church of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established as the dominant religious institution of the realm following the Blinding of 994.

Its seat is the Cathedral of the White Dawn in Velikoye, the first major stone structure in the capital to be retrofitted with roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges to accommodate Owl-folk worshippers and clergy.

The Church teaches that the Blinding was not a catastrophe but a divine illumination — a revelation sent by the White Dawn to transform and elevate the people of Moscavia into vessels of nocturnal wisdom.

Its clergy consists entirely of Owl-folk, drawn predominantly from Snowy Owl-folk bloodlines, and organized into a hierarchy of deacons, priests, bishops, and the Supreme Prelate who serves as the Church's spiritual head.

The Church holds that the natural nocturnal rhythms of the Owl-folk reflect the divine order intended for all creation, and that the long northern nights are sacred periods of communion between the faithful and the White Dawn.

Its doctrine rejects the notion that the Blinding was an act of punishment or random magic, instead asserting that every transformed soul was individually chosen and blessed by the White Dawn to serve as stewards of the frozen north.

The Church maintains a network of parish churches and chapels across Moscavia, each retrofitted with roosting accommodations, and conducts its primary services at night to align with the nocturnal nature of its congregants.

The Winter Solstice Vigil is the Church's most sacred observance, marking the longest night of the year as the moment when the White Dawn burns brightest in the spiritual realm, and the faithful gather in unbroken vigil through three days of prayer and ceremony.

The Church's liturgy incorporates runic inscriptions carved into stone and bone, believed to channel the White Dawn's light into physical blessings, and its rune-practitioners work closely with the Order of the Talon-Scribe.

Human converts who were not transformed during the Blinding are permitted to worship in Church chapels but may not hold clerical rank, a policy justified by the doctrine of unbroken bloodline sanctity.

The Church traces its theological roots to pre-Blinding human Christianity as practiced in Moscavia, but its current doctrine and liturgy were substantially reformed in the years following 994 to incorporate Owl-folk spirituality and the theology of illumination.

Its Supreme Prelate serves as a member of the Night Court by right, advising the Tsar on matters of spiritual governance and moral law, and the Church's teachings carry significant weight in the Tsardom's legal code.

facts.text: The Church of the White Dawn is the state church of the Tsardom of Moscavia, seated at the Cathedral of the White Dawn in the capital city of Velikoye.

Founded in the centuries before the Blinding, the Church was originally a human institution devoted to the veneration of the Dawn, understood as the primordial force that drives back the darkness and renews the world each morning.

The Church underwent a profound transformation after the Blinding of 994, as its clergy and much of its congregation were converted into Owl-folk overnight, forcing a complete reimagining of its liturgy, architecture, and relationship to the passage of time.

The Cathedral of the White Dawn in Velikoye was the first major stone structure in the city to be retrofitted with Owl-folk accommodations, receiving wide landing ledges, heated roosting alcoves, and talon-gripping surfaces at every window by order of the Church's Hierophant in 996.

The Church teaches that the Dawn — the first light of each day — is the visible manifestation of a sacred principle it calls 'Svetyashchiy', the Illuminator, a force that exists in tension with the eternal darkness and whose daily victory over it sustains all life.

The Church holds that every soul, whether born human or Owl-folk, carries within it a spark of Svetyashchiy, and that this spark is what connects the living to the dead, the waking to the sleeping, and the light to the dark.

The Church's clergy are organized into a strict hierarchy: Acolytes serve as apprentices; Deacons conduct minor rites and tend to parish flocks; Priests lead congregations and administer the sacraments; Archpriests oversee dioceses; and the Hierophant, elected by the Council of Dawns, serves as the supreme spiritual authority of the faith.

The Church observes seven major holy days throughout the year, each marking a different aspect of the relationship between light and darkness, with the longest celebrations falling in winter when the nights are longest and the Dawn most desperately awaited.

Its most sacred rite, the Matins of Illumination, is performed each morning at the exact moment of sunrise, when the Hierophant or a senior priest lights a great white taper from the eternal flame kept in the Cathedral's inner sanctum and carries it through the nave while the congregation chants the Prayer of Unveiling.

The Church's relationship with the Night Court has been one of cautious cooperation since 995; while the state governs by night, the Church maintains that its morning rites are spiritually essential to the daily renewal of the realm, and Tsar Dmitry IV has respected this balance.

Parish churches across the Tsardom have been gradually retrofitted to accommodate Owl-folk worshippers, with roosting perches installed along the walls and upper galleries modified to allow flight, though the morning-oriented liturgy remains fundamentally oriented toward the rising sun.

The Church maintains a network of monastic communities called 'Svyatogory' — the Holy Hills — located in remote forest clearings and mountain valleys across Moscavia, where monks and nuns devote themselves to contemplation, rune-working, and the preservation of pre-Blinding theological texts.

elsewhere.text: The Cathedral of the White Dawn, the spiritual heart of the Church of the White Dawn, stands on the eastern slope of the city's highest bluff, its pale stone walls visible from the Khorol River and its bell tower equipped with wide landing ledges that have made it a favored roosting site for members of the Frostwing Host on their nighttime patrols.

The Cathedral houses the eternal flame of Svetyashchiy in its inner sanctum, a fire that has burned without interruption since the Church's founding centuries before the Blinding, and whose light is carried into the world each morning during the Matins of Illumination.

The Church of the White Dawn serves as the spiritual foundation of Moscavian national identity, its teachings on the sacred nature of light and renewal providing a theological framework that has helped the realm navigate the profound social changes wrought by the Blinding.

facts.text: The Church of the White Dawn is the state church of the Tsardom of Moscavia, seated at the Cathedral of the White Dawn in the capital city of Velikoye.

It was established as the dominant religious institution of Moscavia long before the Blinding of 994, though its theology and practices have since been adapted to reflect the transformation of the realm's population.

The Church teaches that the Blinding was a divine act of revelation, in which the northern light — the White Dawn — chose to remake the people of Moscavia in the image of the great owls of the Frostmere Glaciers, creatures long revered in Moscavian spiritual tradition.

Its clergy consists almost exclusively of Snowy Owl-folk, who occupy the highest ranks of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, from the High Bishop seated in Velikoye to the parish priests who serve the rural dioceses across the Tsardom.

The Cathedral of the White Dawn, the Church's seat, was the first major stone building in Velikoye to be retrofitted with talon-gripping ledges and roosting alcoves after the Blinding, setting a precedent for all public architecture in the capital.

The Church's liturgical calendar revolves around the northern seasons, with the longest night of the year — the Winter Solstice Vigil — serving as its most sacred observance, drawing pilgrims from every corner of the Tsardom.

Its theology incorporates elements of pre-Blinding Christian orthodoxy, blended with older Moscavian animistic reverence for the frozen wilderness, the aurora borealis, and the owl as a spirit animal of wisdom and passage between worlds.

The Church maintains a network of rural parishes staffed by itinerant priests who travel between remote villages by flight during the long winter nights, conducting services by firelight in community halls rather than dedicated church buildings.

The Church's doctrine of the Unbroken Bloodline holds that those Owl-folk who descended from four Moscavian grandparents possess the purest spiritual connection to the White Dawn, a teaching that reinforces the broader social hierarchy of the Tsardom.

Its monks and nuns practice a form of nocturnal contemplation known as the Vigil of Still Wings, during which they perch motionless on the cathedral's bell tower for hours, meditating on the silence of the northern sky.

The Church has historically served as a bridge between the human and Owl-folk populations, offering spiritual guidance to both communities while subtly encouraging the cultural assimilation of remaining humans into Owl-folk society.
The High Bishop of the Church sits on the Night Court by right, providing a religious voice in the Tsardom's governance and ensuring that ecclesiastical law is harmonized with secular decree.

elsewhere.text: The Cathedral of the White Dawn, located in the heart of Velikoye, serves as the seat of the Church of the White Dawn, the state church of Moscavia.

The Cathedral of the White Dawn stands as the spiritual heart of Velikoye, its white stone spires visible from the frozen banks of the Khorol River and its bell tower equipped with wide landing ledges for the Snowy Owl-folk who make up the majority of its congregants.

The Church of the White Dawn, as the Tsardom's state church, plays a central role in legitimizing the Night Court's authority, having blessed the governance of every Tsar since Dmitry IV's ascension in the aftermath of the Blinding.

facts.text: The Church of the White Dawn is the state church of the Tsardom of Moscavia, seated at the Cathedral of the White Dawn in the capital city of Velikoye.
Founded centuries before the Blinding, the Church originally served the human population of Moscavia as a Christian institution rooted in northern liturgical traditions.
After the transformation of 994, the Church underwent a profound doctrinal and liturgical reform to accommodate the Owl-folk majority, while maintaining its core theological commitments.

The Church teaches that the Blinding was a divine event — a revelation of God's will for the northern peoples — though it does not claim the transformation was punishment or blessing, but rather a mystery to be reverenced.
Its theology holds that the Snowy Owl-folk are not a new creation but a *revealed* form, that the feather and the talon are as sacred as the flesh and bone that preceded them.
The Church's liturgical calendar follows the natural rhythms of the northern year, with its highest feast days falling during the long winter nights of December and January.
The High Bishop of the Church of the White Dawn holds a seat on the Night Court as a matter of tradition, advising the Tsar on matters of conscience and public morals.

Every parish church in the Tsardom, by Church decree aligned with the Roosting Perch Mandate, is fitted with wide landing ledges, heated roosting alcoves, and talon-gripping stonework at every window.
The Church administers to both Owl-folk and the remaining human population, though its clergy are now exclusively Owl-folk, a transition completed by the year 998.

Baptism and the Rite of First Flight are considered the two sacraments of passage in the Church, the latter performed on young Owl-folk when they take their first sustained flight from the cathedral bell tower.
The Church maintains a network of trained Eared Owl-folk who serve as confessors and spiritual counselors, valued for their empathy and diplomatic temperament.

facts.text: The Northern Postal Authority is the Tsardom of Moscavia's primary postal service, responsible for the collection, sorting, transport, and delivery of written correspondence across the northern provinces.

Headquartered in Velikoye, the Authority operates from a converted granary on the eastern bank of the Khorol River, its stone walls retrofitted with roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges to accommodate its overwhelmingly Owl-folk workforce.

The Authority employs approximately two hundred couriers, the vast majority of whom are Snowy Owl-folk, with a smaller contingent of mixed-lineage Owl-folk serving as ground-based sorters and clerks in the major relay stations.

All correspondence is sorted by region and priority at the Velikoye central office before being loaded into courier satchels for overnight flights to the provincial relay stations, which then redistribute mail to local towns and villages.

Couriers are expected to deliver every letter in their satchel in good condition, with late deliveries and damaged correspondence both subject to formal reprimand; Vasha has never once received either.

The Authority maintains eleven relay stations across the northern provinces, each staffed by a stationmaster and at least two couriers, with supply caches of dried fish, seed cakes, and birch-tar lantern fuel stored in weatherproof lockers.

Every courier of the Northern Postal Authority swears the Oath of the Swift Wing upon entering service: to deliver faithfully, to fly without rest when duty demands, and to protect the contents of every letter as though it were their own.

During winter months, when the Khorol River freezes and the ice road becomes the primary overland route, the Authority coordinates with military escorts to protect couriers carrying sensitive government dispatches from bandits operating along the frozen waterway.

The Authority's annual review, held each spring in Velikoye, evaluates courier performance based on delivery times, condition of returned satchels, and reports from local stationmasters; Vasha has placed in the top three every year since his hiring.

Couriers are issued a standardized leather satchel fitted with a reinforced buckle that can be sealed with the Authority's wax insignia, a small snowflake pressed into deep blue sealant; breaking a sealed satchel is considered a serious breach of postal protocol.

The Authority's senior administrator, Dmitri Volkov, maintains strict discipline across the ranks while also advocating for better equipment and pay for couriers, a balance that has earned him grudging respect even from those who find his manner brusque.

elsewhere.text: Dmitri Volkov, a senior Snowy Owl-folk administrator, heads the Northern Postal Authority in Velikoye, overseeing the operations of two hundred couriers across the northern provinces with a reputation for strict discipline and a quiet commitment to his staff's welfare.

Vasha works as a mail courier for the Northern Postal Authority, delivering correspondence between Velikoye and the outlying towns of the northern provinces; he has consistently placed in the top three at the Authority's annual spring review since joining in 998.

facts.text: The Northern Postal Authority is the primary mail and courier service of the Tsardom of Moscavia, responsible for the collection, sorting, transport, and delivery of correspondence throughout the northern provinces.

Headquartered in Velikoye, the Authority operates from a fortified stone building on the eastern bank of the Khorol River, its offices equipped with roosting perches at every window in accordance with the decree of the night court.

The Authority employs approximately two hundred couriers of various Owl-folk lineages, though its senior administrative positions are held exclusively by Snowy Owl-folk, in keeping with the Night Court's preference for pure-line bloodlines in matters of state governance.

Couriers are organized into regional circuits, with each circuit covering a defined network of towns and settlements; the northernmost circuits are considered the most demanding due to harsh winter conditions and vast distances between population centers.

Every courier of the Northern Postal Authority takes an oath upon employment to deliver all correspondence entrusted to them in a timely and undamaged state, with penalties for tardiness or carelessness ranging from docked pay to dismissal from the service.

The Authority maintains relay stations at key points along major trade routes, where couriers can exchange satchels with fresh colleagues and continue deliveries without interruption, allowing urgent correspondence to travel hundreds of miles in a single night.

Letters and packages are sorted by urgency and destination at the Velikoye central hub, where a team of administrative owls processes incoming and outgoing mail around the clock in eight-hour shifts synchronized with the natural sleep cycles of Owl-folk.

The Authority's couriers are trained in basic self-defense, including the use of short recurve bows fired from mid-flight, a skill developed in response to the threat of banditry along remote northern routes following the Blinding.

Annual reviews of courier performance are conducted in late autumn, before the worst of the winter freeze sets in, and include assessments of delivery accuracy, condition of returned satchels, and peer evaluations from fellow couriers.

The Authority's budget is allocated by the Night Court as part of the annual state spending review, with funding adjusted based on the volume of mail traffic and the expansion or contraction of postal routes into newly settled territories.

facts.text: The port cities of the Free Cities of the Southern Reach have developed a vibrant nocturnal culture centered on night markets, evening theaters, and after-dark taverns, which serve as the social backbone of daily life across the confederation.

Street lighting in every city of the Reach is maintained at levels comfortable for nocturnal vision, using a combination of oil lanterns, enchanted phosphorescent stones, and carefully positioned torches along public walkways and harbor districts.

Public buildings in the Reach, including government halls, theaters, and market complexes, feature wider doorways and lower perching ledges to accommodate Owl-folk residents, a standard adopted across all seven cities following the transformation of 994.

Roosting halls with climate-controlled sleeping quarters are now a standard feature of major public buildings, hotels, and some private residences throughout the Reach, providing safe resting spaces for Owl-folk during daylight hours.

The transition to a nocturnal lifestyle has been widely embraced by both Owl-folk and human residents of the Reach, who regard the evening economy not as a hardship but as a cultural enrichment that sets the region apart from the rest of the continent.

Night markets in cities like Velmara and Ashenmere operate from dusk until well past midnight, offering fresh fish, imported spices, handcrafted goods, and street food prepared by vendors from across the continent.

Evening theatrical performances are a cornerstone of Reach social life, with companies in Korrith and Mirraval staging plays and musical performances that draw audiences of both human and Owl-folk citizens.

Taverns and social houses across the Reach remain open throughout the night, catering to the active hours of Owl-folk while also serving late-night human patrons, and have become important venues for community gatherings and informal governance.

The dual-council system, with parallel Night Councils and Day Councils operating in each city, was established in 995 to ensure that governance reflects the needs of both nocturnal and diurnal populations, and has become a model of cooperative self-governance in the confederation.

Architecture in newer buildings across the Reach incorporates open balconies, high ceilings, and wind-channeling designs that allow Owl-folk to move freely through urban spaces, blending practical adaptation with distinctive aesthetic styles.

The Reach's nocturnal culture has made the confederation a popular tourist destination, attracting visitors from across the continent who come to experience the unique atmosphere of cities that are most alive after dark.

Eared Owl-folk have become particularly prominent in the Reach's nocturnal social spaces, where their distinctive appearance and active nighttime habits make them a visible and celebrated part of the culture.

facts.text: The Free Cities of the Southern Reach collectively sustain a culture defined by openness, diversity, and a thriving nocturnal economy, centered on seven port cities along the southern shore of the Greensea Strait.
The cities were established centuries before the Owl-folk transformation as independent maritime trade hubs, their natural harbors making them essential nodes in cross-strait commerce.

The Common Immigration Charter of 997 prohibits discrimination based on lineage, transformation status, or avian form, extending full civic rights to all Owl-folk — a policy unmatched elsewhere on the continent.

Each of the seven cities — Velmara, Thornhaven, Korrith, Ashenmere, Dunwall, Port Solenne, and Mirraval — governs itself independently through its own council while participating in shared trade agreements and mutual defense pacts.
The dual-council system, established in 995, features parallel Night Councils and Day Councils to accommodate the different waking hours of Owl-folk and human residents respectively.

Architecture across the Reach has been modified to suit Owl-folk residents: buildings feature wider doorways, lower perching ledges, and climate-controlled roosting halls, while public streets are illuminated at levels comfortable for nocturnal vision.

The nocturnal economy is the social backbone of daily life, with night markets, evening theaters, and after-dark taverns drawing residents of all lineages together in shared commerce and entertainment.
Eared Owl-folk constitute a politically active and visibly prominent segment of the population, drawn by both the immigration charter and the cities' tolerance for mixed-lineage identities.
The total population of roughly 180,000 has grown by a third since the transformation, fueled by migration from the northern continent where Owl-folk face discrimination.
Tourism has emerged as a growing economic pillar, attracting travelers curious about the Reach's multicultural society and its uniquely adapted nocturnal lifestyle.

Festivals in the Reach typically span both day and night, with celebratory events scheduled to accommodate all residents regardless of their waking hours, a practice that has become a point of civic pride.

elsewhere.text: The Charter is regarded by residents of the Reach as the foundational legal document that defines the confederation's identity as a haven for diverse lineages.
The Owl-folk transformation of 994, which altered the biology of every human on the northern continent, created a mass displacement that the Reach's open policies were uniquely positioned to address.

facts.text: Blinding Studies is the scholarly discipline centred on explaining the origin, nature, and consequences of the Blinding of 994, the cataclysmic event that transformed the human population of the Tsardom of Moscavia into Owl-folk in a single day.
The field is primarily conducted at the Nocturnal Institute of Velikoye, which was established within the first year after the Blinding to organize research into the event.

Scholars of Blinding Studies investigate the searing flash of light that engulfed the Tsardom, its physical and metaphysical properties, and the mechanism by which human bodies were reshaped into those of great owls.
A central question in the field concerns why the transformation was selective: only humans with at least one Moscavian grandparent were affected, leaving those of purely foreign descent unchanged.

Practitioners of the discipline employ a range of methods, including analysis of surviving eyewitness accounts, examination of pre-Blinding and post-Blinding runic inscriptions, and comparative study of the physiological and cultural changes wrought by the transformation.

The field has given rise to several competing schools of thought, each offering a different explanation for the Blinding's cause, from natural magical phenomena to divine intervention to deliberate rune-working gone awry.

Blinding Studies scholars hold that the event was not merely a biological transformation but a fundamental reordering of the relationship between Moscavia and the natural world, as evidenced by the Owl-folk's nocturnal adaptation and their enhanced affinity for runic magic.

Research findings in Blinding Studies have practical implications for governance, as the Night Court and the Frostwing Host have both drawn upon the Institute's work to inform policy and military strategy.

The Institute maintains a vast archive of pre-Blinding documents, post-Blinding testimony, and rune surveys collected across the Tsardom, making it one of the most important repositories of Moscavian historical knowledge.

Graduates of the Nocturnal Institute who specialize in Blinding Studies often go on to serve as advisors to the Night Court, as their expertise illuminates the legal and social ramifications of the transformation.

The field remains deeply relevant in the year 1000, as the Tsardom continues to grapple with the cultural and political legacy of the Blinding, and new discoveries in runic magic frequently shed fresh light on the event's mechanics.

elsewhere.text: The Institute's Blinding Studies department is its oldest and most prestigious division, established to preserve and analyze knowledge of the 994 transformation before it was lost to living memory.

facts.text: Blinding Studies is the scholarly discipline devoted to understanding the causes, mechanisms, and consequences of the Blinding of 994, the event that transformed the human population of the Tsardom of Moscavia into Owl-folk in a single, catastrophic moment.

The field encompasses natural philosophy, metaphysical inquiry, historical analysis, and rune-working research, drawing on every academic tradition available in the Tsardom to explain what most scholars agree was not a natural occurrence.

At its heart, Blinding Studies asks three central questions: what energy or force produced the blinding light; why did it affect only humans with Moscavian ancestry; and whether the transformation was a punishment, a blessing, or an indifferent cosmic event that simply happened.

Practitioners of the field are called Blinding Scholars, and they are typically Owl-folk who underwent the transformation themselves and thus possess firsthand experience of the event's physical effects, which they bring to their research.

The Nocturnal Institute of Velikoye serves as the principal seat of Blinding Studies, housing the largest archive of pre-Blinding and post-Blinding texts, runic inscriptions, and oral histories in the realm.

Scholars in the field employ a range of methods, including the study of the Frostmere Runic Array's readings from the night of the Blinding, analysis of physical remains from pre-transformation human bodies, and comparative study of the rune-working traditions that predated the event.

The field is organized into several schools of thought, the oldest of which is the Invocationist school, which holds that the Blinding was the result of a deliberate act of immense power—whether divine, arcane, or otherwise—and seeks to identify the agent behind it.

A second major school, the Resonance Theory, proposes that the Blinding was triggered by a natural but unprecedented convergence of runic energy within the Frostmere Glaciers, which resonated with the bloodline of every human carrying Moscavian ancestry, forcing a physical metamorphosis.

A third, more controversial school—the Naturalist Reinterpretation—argues that the Blinding was not supernatural at all but rather a biological event, perhaps triggered by an airborne agent or a mutation carried in the blood of the Moscavian line, which was activated by an unknown environmental catalyst.

Blinding Scholars publish their findings in the quarterly journal *Ochki Nochnoye* (The Night's Eye), which circulates among the Academy of the Chiseled Moon, the Talon-Scribe Order, and the Night Court, whose members take a close interest in the field's discoveries.

The field remains deeply contentious, with no single theory commanding universal acceptance, and scholars frequently clash in public debates held at the Nocturnal Institute, where plumage signaling and vocalization are used alongside spoken argument.

elsewhere.text: The Nocturnal Institute of Velikoye, founded in 995 on the order of Tsar Dmitry IV himself, is a sprawling complex of stone halls and frozen courtyards nestled within Velikoye's inner quarter, its architecture originally built for human scholars and later adapted—with wider doorways, taller ceilings, and reinforced flooring for taloned feet—by Owl-folk architects.

The Institute houses the Department of Blinding Studies as its oldest and most prestigious academic division, staffed by senior scholars who hold the title of Night-Eye Fellows and who advise both the Night Court and the Talon-Scribe Order on matters pertaining to the Blinding.
The Blinding is the foundational event of the entire field; every theory, methodology, and debate in Blinding Studies exists in direct response to the questions it raised.

Members of the Night Court, including Chief Scribe Koroleva, have taken a direct interest in the findings of Blinding Studies, as understanding the Blinding is considered essential to the long-term governance of a realm where the majority of citizens were not born human.

p5.block:
[world]
In narration and dialogue, call things by their everyday names: where a name is followed by "usually called ...", use that name, and keep the full name for formal moments.
Goal: Vasha must deliver a sealed letter to the Chief Scribe of the Talon-Scribe Order at the Academy, navigating the unfamiliar halls of a human-built institution retrofitted for Owl-folk.
Place: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon (usually called the Academy)
- Located in Velikoye's inner quarter, this stone hall serves as the primary training ground and archive for rune-working in the Tsardom.
- The Academy's archives occupy the lower level, a labyrinth of climate-controlled stone chambers that hold copies of every rune pattern approved for public use across the Tsardom, stored in iron-bound cases to protect them from moisture and magical interference.
- The Academy's bell tower, topped with a crescent moon weathervane, is one of the tallest structures in Velikoye's inner quarter and serves as a navigational landmark for nighttime patrols.
- Inside, the great hall opens into a vaulted chamber with pillars carved to resemble owl talons gripping bundles of grain, a motif representing the Order's dual mandate of magical stewardship and agricultural protection.
- A massive stone hall of pale granite, the Academy rises three stories above Velikoye's inner quarter, its facade carved with overlapping crescent moons and spiraling glyph-work that catches the moonlight in shifting silver patterns.
- The building was originally constructed as the Velikoye Rune Academy in 981 by human scholars, who systematized rune-working into written doctrine before the Blinding rendered them unable to practice.
- The central courtyard, enclosed by colonnades, serves as the primary training ground where novice scribes spend their three-year apprenticeship practicing on rows of designated training stones that line the flagstones in concentric circles.
- The Academy's kitchens operate around the clock to feed its resident population, which includes roughly sixty apprentice scribes, thirty registered scribes, and the Chief Scribe's administrative staff, all of whom live on the premises during their active service.
- The entrance is marked by a broad archway of dark basalt, above which the Order's motto — 'By Talon and Stone, the Land Endures' — is chiseled in letters three feet tall, attributed to the first Chief Scribe appointed under Tsar Dmitry IV.
- A small chapel dedicated to the old stone-worship traditions stands in the Academy's southeast corner, maintained for the rare human visitors and as a reminder of the craft's pre-Blinding roots.
- After the Blinding of 994, the Academy was retrofitted with talon-gripping ledges, roosting perches, and widened corridors to accommodate Owl-folk practitioners, transforming it from a human institution into the headquarters of the Talon-Scribe Order.
- By the Scribing Decree of 998, the Academy serves as the centralized authority for approving new rune designs, training registered scribes, and coordinating the maintenance of all public inscriptions within the Tsardom.

What this scene touches: keep what these say true, and bring it in only where the scene calls for it.
Velikoye (capital, usually called the capital)
- The fortified capital city on the banks of the Khorol River, Velikoye has served as the seat of Moscavian governance since before the Blinding.
- The Night Court convenes in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's Palace in Velikoye, which has been specially modified with roosting perches and talon-gripping ledges at every window to accommodate the Owl-folk advisors who serve upon it.
- The fashion for wattles has become so widespread among Velikoye's Owl-folk population that the Nightmarket now includes a dedicated 'Wattle Row' among its nocturnal stalls.
- Velikoye, the capital of Moscavia, served as the seat of governance both before and after the Blinding, though its architecture and daily life were thoroughly adapted to suit the nocturnal Owl-folk who now dominated its population.
- Velikoye's most prominent church, the Cathedral of the White Dawn, was the first major stone structure in the city to be retrofitted with Owl-folk accommodations after the Blinding, its bell tower now equipped with wide landing ledges and heated roosting alcoves.
- The city's population of approximately forty thousand is now split roughly between Snowy Owl-folk and the remaining human inhabitants, with a smaller number of Eared Owl-folk who serve as interpreters and diplomats at the borders.
- In 999: Wattles have become so ubiquitous in Velikoye that the Nightmarket now hosts a dedicated Wattle Row, a narrow street lined entirely with wattlemaker stalls open from dusk until dawn.
- In 999: The Nightmarket's Wattle Row opens, formalizing the wattle trade and signaling its full acceptance into Velikoye's daily life.

Runic Magic of the Tsardom (magic, usually called Rune-working)
- A discipline of carved stone script that predates the Blinding and now flourishes under Owl-folk stewardship, runic magic draws its power from the northern land's mineral veins and frozen rivers, practiced primarily by dedicated scribes who serve both secular and spiritual purposes within Moscavian society.
- The Blinding disrupted rune-working across the Tsardom as human practitioners were transformed, leaving many carved sites dormant until Owl-folk scribes learned the craft.
- Tsar Dmitry IV issued the Scribing Decree, formally establishing the Order of the Talon-Scribe to preserve rune-lore and maintain public inscriptions.
- Owl-folk scribes use talon-tips as focusing tools, pressing them into wet clay rune-molds before transferring the design to stone.
- The Blinding is sometimes attributed to a failed rune-casting of catastrophic proportions, though mainstream scholars reject this theory as superstition.
- The first known rune-stone was erected at the mouth of the Khorol River, marking territory and warding against marsh spirits.
- In 998: By the Scribing Decree of 998, the Academy serves as the centralized authority for approving new rune designs, training registered scribes, and coordinating the maintenance of all public inscriptions within the Tsardom.
- In 998: Under the Scribing Decree of 998, the Frostmere Array is classified as a Tier-One Public Site, meaning its maintenance is overseen directly by the Grand Chiseler and funded through the Tsardom's general treasury rather than local provincial budgets.

Tsardom of Moscavia (nation, usually called Moscavia)
- A sovereign northern realm transformed six years ago when millions of its human inhabitants became Owl-folk in a single inexplicable event, the Tsardom of Moscavia is now ruled by Snowy Owl-folk from its fortified capital of Velikoye, its society and institutions reshaped to accommodate nocturnal governance and avian bodies.
- Moscavia's borders are defined to the north by the Frostmere Glaciers, to the east by the Ashwood Marshes, to the south by the Greensea Strait, and to the west by the Greenwall Mountains, which separate it from the neighboring kingdom of Valdren.
- The Tsardom is governed from Velikoye by a Tsar (currently Tsar Dmitry IV), who rules with the counsel of a night court that conducts its sessions after sundown to accommodate the nocturnal nature of the ruling Owl-folk.
- The current ruler of the Tsardom, Tsar Dmitry IV presides over the Night Court from his palace in Velikoye and holds ultimate authority over all matters of state.
- Tsar Dmitry IV issued the Night Court Decree, mandating that all governance would take place after sundown to accommodate the Owl-folk's nocturnal nature.
- The Frostwing Host serves as the primary military arm of the Tsardom of Moscavia, its all-Owl-folk composition reflecting the fundamental transformation of the realm's population since the Blinding of 994.
- In 999: The Nightmarket's Wattle Row opens, formalizing the wattle trade and signaling its full acceptance into Velikoye's daily life.
- In 999: Every spring, the Order conducts the Rune Census, a province-wide survey in which registered scribes inspect all public inscriptions for signs of wear, corruption, or interference, and file reports with the Academy in Velikoye.

Northern Postal Authority (institution)
- In 998: Vasha works as a mail courier for the Tsardom of Moscavia's postal service, a role that takes him between Velikoye and the outlying towns of the northern provinces.

Moscavian Owl-folk (people, usually called Owl-folk)
- The Moscavian Owl-folk originated six years ago in the year 994, when a sudden blinding light engulfed every human with at least one Moscavian grandparent, transforming them into their current form.
- Eared owl forms are more common among those with only one Moscavian grandparent, and they appear predominantly in neighboring countries beyond the Tsardom of Moscavia.
- The transformation of 994 occurred simultaneously throughout the Tsardom of Moscavia and its neighboring territories, turning millions of humans into Owl-folk in a single, inexplicable event that scholars continue to study without definitive answers.
- The Moscavian Owl-folk dominate the civic and religious institutions of Velikoye, their unbroken bloodlines lending them social prestige that shapes the city's governance and daily life.
- The transformation was instantaneous and irreversible, sparing no one who met the bloodline criterion regardless of age, location, or consent.
- The Owl-folk retain the full intelligence, memories, and personalities of their former human lives, but now resemble large owls standing between three and four feet tall.
- In 997: The Night Court Decree of 997 formalized Plumage Signaling as an accepted mode of testimony and response during court proceedings, requiring human intermediaries to be trained in its interpretation.
- In 998: Misread signals can lead to diplomatic incidents within the Night Court; in 998, a misunderstanding over an advisor's half-spread wing during a border dispute nearly escalated tensions with the Kerensky Principality before the misinterpretation was corrected.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe (order, usually called Talon-Scribe Order)
- An institution of state-appointed Owl-folk rune-practitioners who maintain public inscriptions across the Tsardom and advise the Night Court on magical matters, headquartered in the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velikoye.
- The Corrupted Rune Site Investigation branch falls under the Order's broader mandate to maintain public inscriptions and advise the Night Court on magical matters, reporting directly to the Chief Scribe in Velikoye.
- Tsar Dmitry IV founds the Night Court in response to the Blinding, establishing nocturnal governance for the transformed realm.
- All members of the Order are Owl-folk, as the Blinding of 994 rendered human practitioners unable to practice rune-working and the craft was subsequently mastered by transformed scribes.
- The Order's central administration is housed in the stone hall known as the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in the inner quarter of Velikoye, where the institution's archives hold copies of every rune pattern approved for public use.
- The Order's highest-ranking member is the Chief Scribe, a title appointed by the Tsar from among the most experienced and politically trusted Owl-folk practitioners in the realm.
- In 998: Tsar Dmitry IV issues the Scribing Decree, formally establishing the Order of the Talon-Scribe to preserve rune-lore and mandate public inscription maintenance.
- In 998: Corrupted Rune Site Investigation is a specialized branch of the Talon-Scribe Order's work, tasked with identifying, cataloging, and remedying rune inscriptions that have fallen into disrepair or been tampered with since the era of human practitioners.

Who is here, by heritage (keep every description and action true to these bodies and instincts):
- Vasha (Snowy Moscavian Owl-folk, a race of Moscavian Owl-folk): His eyes are a striking deep blue, a color notably different from the pale yellow or amber typical of most Snowy Owl-folk. He was born in owl form in the year 996 to two pure-line Snowy Owl-folk parents in the town of Murom, making him a member of the first generation born entirely as Owl-folk. His nocturnal instincts are keenly developed, allowing him to navigate dark winter nights and read letters by moonlight with ease, though he keeps a small lantern for the rare cloudy evenings. His plumage is nearly all white, with only the faintest traces of gray visible along the tips of his flight feathers when examined closely in strong light. They are the most visually uniform subgroup of Owl-folk, as the snowy owl phenotype is expressed almost universally among pure-line descendants, with very few exhibiting significant deviations such as ear tufts or dark markings. Among the youngest generation, born entirely in owl form, the pure-line Snowy Owl-folk exhibit the most consistent physical resemblance to one another of any Owl-folk subgroup, having never known the variability of mixed human lineages. Their talons are notably large and powerful for their body size, an adaptation that has proven useful for both locomotion and gripping objects in place of hands. Eared owl forms are more common among those with only one Moscavian grandparent, and they appear predominantly in neighboring countries beyond the Tsardom of Moscavia. Their wingspans range from eight to nine feet, allowing them limited but functional flight over short distances and low altitudes. The Owl-folk retain the full intelligence, memories, and personalities of their former human lives, but now resemble large owls standing between three and four feet tall. Instincts: Despite their transformed bodies, they experience human emotions, hunger, thirst, and the need for social connection, though their social bonds have shifted to accommodate their new physical needs.
[end of world]

turns.direction: Vasha is shown inside and led through the Academy toward the Chief Scribe's office; show what he sees and who he passes.
turns.output:
The entrance hall swallows the sound of his landing whole. Vasha's talons click against pale granite as he walks forward, his gaze sweeping the chamber. The talon-gripping ledges mounted on the walls are spaced at odd intervals—some clearly retrofitted after the fact, their iron brackets crudely bolted into stone that predates them by a decade, while others seem more deliberately placed, as if the original human architects had anticipated something they couldn't name. A pair of apprentice scribes in pale linen wraps pause near one of the grain-pillar columns, their heads tilted in quiet conversation, talon-slates held against their chests. One of them—a stocky Snowy Owl with a faint dusting of gray along her breast feathers—nods in his direction as he passes, and he returns the gesture with a slight dip of his head.

The corridor beyond the great hall stretches long and dimly lit, oil lamps set into wall sconces casting warm circles of amber across the flagstones. The air shifts as he walks—warmer now, carrying the unmistakable scent of heated wax and old parchment, underlaid with something earthier, mineral, like the smell of deep stone. His postal satchel bumps against his flank with each step, the sealed letter inside a small but insistent weight. He's been to Velikoye before on delivery runs, but never inside the Academy itself. The Northern Postal Authority's usual business with the Order is conducted through a drop-box near the eastern gate, manned by a clerk who never looked him in the eye.

He rounds a corner and nearly collides with a broad-shouldered Snowy Owl standing at a desk set into an alcove, reviewing a stack of papers pinned beneath a carved wooden block. The bird's plumage is mostly white with a faint blush of tawny gold at the wingtips, and his expression—sharp, appraising—suggests he is not the sort one keeps waiting. A brass nameplate on the desk reads REGISTRATION DESK — INTERNAL COURIERS & VISITORS. Vasha adjusts course, approaching with the easy, unhurried stride of someone accustomed to navigating unfamiliar places.

"You'll want to state your business and your origin," the desk-keeper says, not looking up from his papers.

turns.direction: The Chief Scribe breaks the seal and reads the letter in front of Vasha; it concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol, and she tells him what it means.
turns.output:
The desk-keeper's talons tap a slow rhythm against the wooden block as he finishes reviewing his papers, then finally lifts his head. His deep yellow eyes fix on Vasha with the kind of look that says he's already decided this won't take long.

"Name and posting. And the letter's destination within the building—don't just say 'Chief Scribe,' give me the office."

Vasha shifts his weight, talons clicking against the flagstone. He's handled packages for the Academy before, of course—the drop-box at the eastern gate sees plenty of Northern Postal Authority traffic—but never anything flagged for direct delivery. The secondary seal on this one, that crescent moon bisected by a line, has been bothering him since he picked it up in Murom three days ago. He reaches into his satchel with a careful talon and produces the letter, its black wax seal still intact, the postal authority's stamp pressed cleanly into the surface. The desk-keeper examines it, turns it once, then nods and disappears through a side door behind the alcove.

He returns a minute later with a lean, silver-plumaged Snowy Owl whose bearing carries the unmistakable weight of seniority. She's older—born human, clearly, though the transformation has smoothed any traces of the original face into the sharp, angular features common to the first generation. Her eyes are a pale, almost colorless amber, and they settle on the letter in Vasha's grip with immediate recognition. She doesn't introduce herself, doesn't greet him. She simply holds out one talon and says, "Give it here." The desk-keeper melts back into the shadows of the alcove as if he'd never existed. The Chief Scribe breaks the seal with a single precise motion, unfolds the parchment, and reads—standing right where she is, not inviting Vasha to sit, not offering any warmth at all. Her eyes move across the page twice, then lift to his. "You're the courier who brought this from Murom." It isn't a question. She folds the letter carefully and holds it against her chest with one talon. "This concerns a rune-stone at the mouth of the Khorol. The first one ever carved, if the archives have their history right."

turns.direction: Vasha is shown inside and led through the Academy toward the Chief Scribe's office; show what he sees and who he passes.
turns.output:
The entrance hall swallows the sound of his landing like a stone drinking water. Vasha's talons click against the flagstones as he crosses toward the far wall, where a wide corridor branches left past a row of roosting alcoves—each one fitted with a padded perch and a small desk, clearly meant for scribes to rest between duties. A pair of apprentice scribes pass him going the other way, their training slates tucked under their wings, and one of them—a young Snowy Owl-folk barely two years out of fledging, if Vasha's eye is right—stops short at the sight of him. The apprentice's head tilts in that involuntary way all young Owl-folk do when something catches their attention, and Vasha gives a small dip of his head in acknowledgment before moving on. The corridor ahead narrows and widens in an uneven rhythm, the original human proportions still visible in the way doorframes sit too high for comfortable entry without a hop, while the added ledges and perches jut from the walls at angles that look afterthoughts bolted onto centuries of stonework.

He follows the sound of footsteps and the faint glow of mounted candles deeper into the Academy. The walls here are lined with iron-bound cases—some barely a foot tall, others stretching nearly to the ceiling—and behind their glass faces he catches glimpses of carved stone slabs covered in rune patterns, each one etched with a precision that speaks of years of practice. A registered scribe, identifiable by the silver crescent pinned to her breast feathers, rounds the corner ahead of him carrying a stack of documents in her talons, and she pauses at the sight of the satchel slung across Vasha's chest. She looks at the postal seal, then at his face, then back at the seal, her amber eyes narrowing with professional curiosity.

"Courier?" she asks, and when Vasha confirms with a nod, she gestures down the corridor with the edge of her wing. "Chief Scribe's office is through the arch with the grain-carving above it—you can't miss it. But fair warning, she's in the middle of reviewing the Rune Census returns from the northern provinces, so she's not exactly in a receiving mood." She shifts the documents to a more secure grip under one wing. "There's a waiting alcove just before the office doors."

turns.direction: The Chief Scribe breaks the seal and reads the letter in front of Vasha; it concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol, and she tells him what it means.
turns.output:
Vasha finds the waiting alcove without difficulty—a shallow niche cut into the corridor wall, furnished with a padded perch and a small table where a half-melted candle gutters in its holder. He settles onto the perch, the satchel warm against his breast, and listens to the sounds of the Academy settling into its nighttime rhythms. Somewhere deeper in the building, a door opens and closes. Footsteps—heavier than any Owl-folk's—cross a stone floor. A murmur of voices, too distant to make out.

After perhaps twenty minutes, the silver-crescent scribe returns and gives him a curt nod. "She'll see you now." She leads him past a pair of heavy oak doors, each carved with a motif of talons gripping sheaves of wheat, and into a chamber that is surprisingly small for a Chief Scribe's office. The walls are lined floor to ceiling with wooden shelves holding rolled parchments and leather-bound volumes. A wide desk sits before a tall arched window, and behind it, perched on a raised chair fitted with a broad sitting ledge, is an older Snowy Owl-folk whose breast feathers have gone soft and cloudy with age. Her deep blue eyes—almost the same shade as Vasha's, he notes—fix on him with an intensity that makes the room feel smaller.

"Leave the satchel on the desk," she says, and before Vasha can even set it down, she has already reached for the letter, breaking the black wax seal with a thumbnail-talon in a single clean motion. She unfurls the parchment, and her eyes move across the page. The candlelight shifts as she tilts the letter, and Vasha catches a glimpse of dense, precise handwriting and a wax stamp at the bottom bearing the Frostmere Array's mark. Her talons tighten on the edges of the parchment. She reads it twice. Then she sets it down on the desk very carefully, as if it were something fragile, and looks up at him.

"This is a report from the Frostmere Array's maintenance team," she says, her voice carrying the measured calm of someone who has delivered and received difficult news many times. "They've found the Khorol's first rune-stone—the oldest inscription in the entire Tsardom, the one that marked the territory before the marshes were drained—corrupted. Not worn, not damaged by weather. Corrupted."

Vasha's talons meet the flagstones with a soft, deliberate click — the sound of a postal courier who knows how to make an entrance without making a scene. To his right, a staircase — human-sized steps augmented with shallow ramps and handholds for taloned feet — leads upward. But directly ahead, past the great pillars, a hallway stretches deeper into the building, wider than the others, lit by iron sconces that hold candles rather than the oil lamps more common in Velikoye's streets. A painted sign hangs from a bracket at the corridor's mouth: Administration — Office of the Chief Scribe, this way. The paint is fresh, the brushwork precise, and someone has carved a small rune beneath the text — a directional ward, subtle enough that most visitors wouldn't notice it, guiding the way with a gentle tug at the edges of perception.

Vasha adjusts his satchel and walks. His talons find the flagstones smooth and well-swept beneath him, the Academy's maintenance crew clearly thorough in their work. The corridor opens into a smaller antechamber where a desk sits beneath a window fitted with talon-grips and heavy shutters, and behind the desk, a young registered scribe — a stout Great Grey Owl-folk with ear tufts that droop like wilted flowers — looks up from a stack of parchment.

turns.direction: The Chief Scribe breaks the seal and reads the letter in front of Vasha; it concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol, and she tells him what it means.

The young scribe behind the desk blinks up at Vasha, then glances at the satchel slung across his chest. "You're from the Northern Postal Authority? The Chief Scribe isn't expecting a courier tonight — or any night, usually. She gets her correspondence through the regular channels." But the secondary seal on the letter — the crescent moon bisected by a line — makes him pause. That mark belongs to the Chief Scribe's own office. Whatever this letter contains, someone in her administration sent it back to her.

He rises from his desk with a stiff, slightly awkward motion — young registered scribes still carry a certain clumsiness about them, their training not yet ironed into the practiced stillness of veteran practitioners. "Wait here," he says, and disappears through a heavy oak door set into the wall behind him, the kind of door that has been reinforced at the top with a talon-grip bar to keep it from swinging shut.

A minute passes. The candle in the nearest sconce gutters and steadies. Then the door opens again, and a figure ducks through the frame — short, broad-shouldered, unmistakable. Chief Scribe Koroleva fills the doorway with a presence that seems larger than her three-foot frame would suggest. Her tawny-brown plumage is immaculate, her breast feathers a soft silvery-grey that catches the candlelight. That lopsided arrangement of her ear tufts — the left one hanging past her jaw, the right standing erect like an exclamation mark — gives her face an expression of perpetual, mild surprise. But her burnt-orange eyes are anything but surprised. They are sharp, searching, fixed on the letter Vasha holds as she crosses the antechamber with quick, purposeful steps. "Bring it here," she says, extending a taloned hand. "And tell me — was there a verbal message accompanying this, or was it sent under silence?"

Vasha places the sealed letter into her outstretched talons. Koroleva carries it to the desk, where she settles onto a carved wooden stool — human furniture, modified with a wider seat and backrest to suit owl bodies — and breaks the black wax seal with a single clean motion of her thumb.
